speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to report on the World Food Conference which began slightly more than two weeks ago in Rome. Last Saturday the conference came to a close, and of the 123 countries represented and the more than 1,200 delegates attending, virtually none did not have impressed upon them the need for increased production by all farmers in the world. While many countries were called on to produce more food and help developing countries to do the same, Canada was among the few that had chosen to give a clear and significant mandate to their representatives at the conference.
Let me say a word about our representatives. Our delegation at Rome was well prepared and was one of the best there, if not the best. We had two federal cabinet ministers, a provincial cabinet minister, three parliamentary observers and representatives of the public service. They all took their responsibilities very seriously and worked hard to achieve positive results. Right here I would like to
set the record straight about one thing. Some people have alleged that our delegation was trying to filibuster in the committee dealing with trade. This is absolutely false. At no time did anyone on the Canadian delegation attempt any type of negative action at the conference. In point of fact, there were fairly extensive exchanges on the trade issue but these were between the delegates of the developing countries that held some very divergent views on the subject.
When my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), made known our willingness to provide a more than proportionate share of the minimum world target for food aid and to more than double contributions to the world food program, there was a good deal of optimism that the turning point of the conference had been reached. The feeling of optimism was increased when Australia made a corresponding offer in response to the example set by Canada. If other countries had done the same, the World Food Conference would have been a greater success.
Everyone with a real interest in farmers and agriculture ought to have the chance to go to a meeting like the World Food Conference. It brings home just how important good farmers and productive, efficient agriculture really are. When I sat in on some of those meetings held in a big building that Mussolini had put up for the 1942 Olympic Games and waited for the translators to catch up to the speaker, or maybe listened to delegates from various countries arguing for 20 minutes whether the right word to use in a sentence was "scarce" or "limited", I had a chance to think about some of the countries that were represented there.
What really struck me was that there were no developed countries that did not have well developed agriculture as the strong foundation for the rest of their economy. If a country's agriculture was not healthy, you could be pretty sure that they were having other problems as well. You could see the same sort of thing with respect to the developing countries. You cannot just lump them all together under that name. Some of them who had not paid enough attention to their farmers and their needs were wishing they had. But you could tell that the countries that were really looking after their agriculture were also going to take off pretty quickly in the rest of their development.
To try to get anything done in those committees was something else again. They would start off with a pretty reasonable draft of a resolution and go at it until it looked like the turkey two days after Thanksgiving dinner. Sometimes I wondered if they would ever get any meat back on the bones. In spite of the difficulties, we did make progress. Our delegation met several times a day to discuss progress and problems in the committees. In this work we

November 22, 1974
World. Food Conference
were helped considerably by Canada's active participation in the preparatory committees.
I would just like to mention here that apart from official government delegation at Rome, Canada was fortunate in having very fine representation fron non-government organizations, or NGOs as they are called. Representatives from our delegation met with them frequently and the discussions were both cordial and useful for all of us. I have nothing but praise for them and the job they did on behalf of their respective organizations.
The facts of Canadian leadership at the conference are as follows: the Canadian food aid pledge helped to move Australia and the EEC into making specific food aid pledges and the United States to accept a ten million tons annual food aid target. Canada drafted the clause ensuring that the Agricultural Development Fund would come into effect when there were substantial new funds and the prospect of continuity. Canada was also one of the first western countries to accept the Agricultural Development Fund. Canada was the only country to pledge 20 per cent of its food aid through multilateral channels, including a 100 per cent increase in Canada's pledge to the world food program for 1975 and 1976.
Canada pushed for a universal exchange of information on crop prospects and inputs. Canada offered to earmark national grain reserves for world food security. Canada led in stressing the importance of fisheries and environmental concerns. Canada has pressed for effective followup to the World Food Conference using existing international agencies that have a proven record of producing results.
At no time did Canada forget the importance of the producer as the key contributor to an adequate food supply. All these are examples of Canadian initiative and leadership at the World Food Conference, but this list is certainly not complete.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
I was approached on many occasions by ministers of agriculture from developing countries who wanted to get bilateral development aid from Canada. They were looking for Canadian agricultural technology to use in their countries because they think Canada has the best technology and the most productive agriculture in the world. They also know that they can get help from Canada without political strings attached, if they are willing to make the effort to help themselves. It is still too early to make an adequate assessment of the World Food Conference. Nonetheless, I believe that there are real reasons for being optimistic. Perhaps the most important of these is that as a result of the conference many countries will start increasing their food production earlier than they would have.
Several resolutions were passed by the plenary session of the conference. However, the accepted wording of the resolutions was made on the basis of oral amendments, and final wordings of the resolutions are not yet available. Most important among the resolutions is the one to establish a fund to be called the international fund for agricultural development. The fund would finance agricultural and fisheries development projects in developing countries. Contributions to it would be on a voluntary basis.

The fact that the resolution's co-sponsors included oil producing nations such as Iran, Kuwait, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Venezuela may be regarded as a commitment by these countries to use some of their financial resources, and we hope they will, to support a multilateral program for agriculture and fisheries development.
The conference has asked the FAO and other concerned international organizations such as the International Wheat Council to make the arrangements necessary for the establishment of a global information and early warning system on food and agriculture. The objectives, policies and guidelines as set out in the text of the proposed FAO international undertaking on world food security were also endorsed by the conference. Governments of major exporting and importing nations have been invited to enter discussions on the feasibility of establishing grain reserves in appropriate locations. The Director General of the FAO has convened a meeting of representatives of interested countries for November 29 to look at the shortterm problems of the developing countries most seriously affected by current food shortages.
The arrangements for follow-up at the conference were covered in a complicated resolution that in effect sets up a world food council at the ministerial level that would report to the United Nations General Assembly through the Economic and Social Council. The World Food Council would serve to co-ordinate follow-up policies concerning food production, nutrition, food security, food trade and food aid. Membership of the World Food Council has yet to be determined, but its members will be nominated by the Economic and Social Council and elected by the United Nations General Assembly.
The conference did recommend, among other things, an FAO committee on world food security, an intergovernmental committee of the World Food Program, and that the board of directors of the international fund for agricultural development should submit periodic reports to the World Food Council. The conference also requested that international groups and organizations take leadership in following up the results of the conference. The conference did adopt a long declaration entitled "Declaration on the eradication of hunger". Its final wording is not yet available, but it is a document that contains the suggestions of many groups that were agreeable to others, and hence is perhaps weaker than we would have liked because of the need for consensus.
Canada's leadership and contribution to the conference is perhaps best summed up in a letter to the Secretary of State for External Affairs dated November 9, from Mr. Aquino, executive director of the World Food Program, as follows:
I would again like to express to you, and through you, also to the Secretary of State for Agriculture, the hon. Mr. Whelan, my own and my colleagues profound gratification for the excellent policy statement which you recently presented to the World Food Conference in Rome on behalf of the government and people of Canada. We in the World Food Program are deeply appreciative of the leading role CIDA has long taken and so clearly intends to continue to take in helping to "seek the elimination of hunger". Your moving speech and very practical undertakings and proposals are certainly most encouraging.
November 22, 1974

I was a proud Canadian before I went to the conference. I am an even prouder a Canadian after attending this conference.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: My office is located in the same building as the minister's, up four flights of stairs, and even if it meant the minister climbing those four flights of stairs, surely we could have received a copy. The minister speaks continually about co-operation in the interests of Canadian and world farmers. If this is any indication of the co-operation he proposes to extend to other nations to meet the world food crisis, then heaven help the world's hungry. The only sympathetic thing I can say is that I, too, would be ashamed to release this statement if I were the minister.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
In his final article on the World Food Conference, Mr. James Rusk, writing in the Globe and Mail, summed it up by saying:
Politics won and food lost. The issues were political, the actions were political and the conclusions were political.
I do not point a finger at the minister, but this is my view of what happened at that conference. I have no way of judging whether the conference was a political success; but in terms of judging whether it was a success in solving the world food crisis, none of us in this house can claim that it was successful. With respect to the position taken by Canada and its participation, I say to the minister and to all hon. members that I was proud to be a Canadian on the second day of that conference. I was proud when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) gave his statement. I think we all had reason to be proud at that particular point.
We went to the conference in the hope of offering leadership. I believe we did that, Mr. Speaker. Our commitment of food aid of one million tons a year for the next three years had two very obvious things to commend it: first, our commitment was expressed in terms of tons rather than dollars, which is what we had been requested to do; second, in comparison with other food exporters I think our tonnage commitment had everything to com-
World Food Conference
mend it. However, there is another yardstick. I do not refer only to the statistical fact that just three or four years ago the tonnage we delivered to the hungry nations far exceeded our Rome commitment: I emphasize that this three-year commitment does not begin until the next crop year. The Montreal Gazette, in an editorial on November 28 had this to say:
The Canadian contribution of one million tons for the next three years is disappointing when weighed against earlier contributions. Canadian refusal to assist with fertilizers is miserly when compared with the 150,000 metric tons given in 1970 and the fact that approximately 30 per cent of Canadian fertilizer production was exported to the United States in the 1973-74 season.
In the same vein, the Globe and Mail said this:
It is impressive only in that it stands out against the shameful background.
The yardstick that I refer to is measuring our assistance in terms of our capacity as Canadians to produce. Measured against that yardstick, no Canadian can take too much satisfaction. If we submit ourselves to that test, we have only to answer the question to read the minister's statement to this House on October 3, 1974, when he said, as reported at page 96 of Hansard:
I have said the farmers of this nation will increase their productivity by 50 per cent in five years if they are given a decent return for what they produce and a guarantee that they will receive the same as the rest of our society wants-
Submitting ourselves to that test of capacity, not one member of the House or one producer in this country can take too much satisfaction. In terms of emergency relief, I noted the question put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs on November 14, a day during which the conference was being held, and the figure of $50 million was thrown around helter-skelter. The only thing I know about this $50 million is that as a result of the conference in Rome there has been a reallocation within the CIDA program of $50 million. There is no new fund. It is no big deal.
May I deal now with what, in my opinion, was the most significant issue from the Canadian viewpoint. That was the necessity of assisting developing countries to increase their own food production. Canadians had every reason to believe that we in the Canadian delegation would offer real leadership. First of all, we looked to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture prior to his leaving for Rome and he indicated that this was our number one priority since we had the leadership and the expertise necessary to assist in this regard. I believe that the most important sentence of the address of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the conference is as follows:
Canada emphatically supports the development of increased food production capacity by developing countries as the key to an anti-hungry strategy.
Similarly, in his speech in the House on November 15 when he listed seven points which he hoped would assist Canada to participate in fighting this crisis, he said, as reported at page 1376 of Hansard:
First, Canada is prepared to accord a high priority in its assistance program to the agricultural development of countries which are mobilizing their own resources to increase food production.
These have been hollow words. We did not exhibit any dramatic leadership in this area; in fact, we have demonstrated no real leadership at all. The conference itself did

November 22, 1974
World Food Conference
not come to grips with this issue. The future for agriculture in developing countries is little or no brighter as a result of the conference. The only ray of hope which the minister mentioned-and I hope it is a ray-is the agricultural development fund, which at this moment is unfunded. The only contribution that Canada makes, I repeat, is the reallocation of $50 million within the CIDA program.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) may wish to take exception to my criticism of this vital aspect of the Rome conference, but I can illustrate my point simply by saying this: if, as he has said repeatedly, we went to Rome expecting a conference on food production, why did Canada's delegation not include at least one person who represented the food producers of Canada? Ministers of the Crown do not produce food; members of parliament do not produce food; public servants do not produce food, and neither do international conferences.
The minister has bragged about-I share his pride in this respect-the tremendous talent available from farm organizations and producer groups in this country, yet not one of them was represented at the conference. Coincidentally, at this conference were two Canadians, Mr. Munro and Mr. Pigeon, both of whom represent producer groups in Canada. But they were there in an international capacity; they were not even invited to informal meetings held by the Canadian delegation until I made a point of seeking their presence at those meetings.
Unhappily, the world must conclude that the conference was not successful in respect of the key issue of food production in developing countries. Canadians must conclude either that we failed to provide leadership in this area or that whatever leadership we intended was not evident to other delegations. Whichever is the case, we must all regret our failure in this one area which we acknowledge to be the most important.
There are two matters I wish to discuss briefly. One is the presence in our delegation of senior members of the public service. It might be said by those more cynical than me that public servants really prove their mettle when they are dealing with ministers whose shortcomings are obvious in certain circumstances. I am not a cynic: I only say that within the framework of their instructions, the responsible public servants of the Department of Agriculture demonstrated an enthusiasm and determination for which I sincerely commend them.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
The other point concerns the members of the non-governmental organizations. I appreciate the minister's comments in his statement. But, unfortunately, that feeling was not unanimous within our delegation and in my opinion there was even the suggestion that their role for future conferences should be questioned. If that role- which to me is a vital and enthusiastic one-is questioned, it should be questioned in this House, and nowhere else, because I believe these people fulfilled a very useful function. I appreciate your restlessness, Mr. Speaker, but anyone who has been a parliamentary observer knows that his function defies job description. I am working off a

little of my frustration right now and hope you will bear with me.
My final point is an obvious one, and because it is so obvious we sometimes lose sight of it. We met in Rome because many people in this world are starving to death and many more are so undernourished that their chances of making a meaningful contribution to society are minimal or non-existent. This was why delegations from so many countries journeyed to Rome. Yet repeatedly at the conference, from our delegation and others I heard the desperately needy countries criticized in private because of the actions of their leaders. This criticism took the form of statements that country "A" was wasting money on expenditures for such things as armaments, money that otherwise could be used to provide more food for its people; country "B" was guilty of graft and corruption in dealing with food aid; country "C" had delegates at the conference who were riding around in Rolls-Royce cars while its people were starving.
All Canadians can take a personal affront at such action, particularly when we talk of countries who are recipients of our aid. All members of parliament can go to their respective ridings and be safe politically for not only criticizing such actions but, indeed, for justifying the withholding of aid because of such immorality. I sensed this personal feeling of effrontery every day at the conference. But what we ignore or forget is that it was not the starving child who was guilty of wasteful government expenditure, it was not the undernourished mother who was guilty of graft and corruption and it was not the worker, who is so underfed that he is non-productive, who is riding around in a Rolls-Royce. I suggest that all of us should resist the natural negative and politically expedient reaction of using such actions as reasons or excuses for withholding assistance. I suggest that these actions, albeit reprehensible, of needy countries should not provide the reason or excuse but, rather, should provide the challenge to us to make our aid more effective. Some 80 per cent of that aid is bilateral, so we can accept this worthy challenge.
In conclusion, may I say that Canadians share our disappointment that the World Food Conference failed to fulfill our aspirations for it. In a positive sense, however, I believe we should feel that the failures of the conference will add to the focus on and the urgency of the world food crisis. If nothing else, the focus on this crisis has provided us, as Canadians, with a dramatic challenge. The Gazette editoral to which I referred, under the heading "The hungry still unfed" states-

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the House in advance for detaining it longer on this matter, but I think this conference was one of tremendous importance and significance. I, too, was a parliamentary observer and I hope the House will bear with me while I make a few remarks on the subject. This World Food Conference was, despite all the cynics and all the pessimists, an historic and significant occasion. It was, of course, dealing with a basic problem of humanity, the problem of food, which includes the age-old problem of malnutrition affecting millions of people, including 200 million children throughout the world. The conference was also dealing with the urgent and immediate problem of threatened starvation on a large scale in some parts of the world, and I mention Bangladesh, India and central Africa.
The conference was watched with hope and anxiety by the whole world. It was historic in the sense that it was the first time representatives of nations had gathered together to apply their minds to this problem. As Pope Paul VI put it in a striking address to the conference: "The food crisis is a crisis of civilization and solidarity." It would obviously be too soon to assess the results of the conference. They will depend on the follow-up and upon whether the nations of the world are prepared to give content to the resolutions they passed by providing the resources and machinery to make them work.
My view is that the conference had both successes and failures. An outstanding failure was in the area of trade. The resolution of the food problem of the world in the long run requires substantial increases in the purchasing power of the least developed countries. The resolution of the conference on this point was disappointingly vague. I want to make one thing clear; there seemed to be universal agreement that this problem could be solved. Nature has provided the means; the question is whether man can provide the wisdom to solve it. There is another observation I want to make, and that is that those who produce surpluses of food must not use those surpluses in an attempt to gain political advantage.
There were several aspects to the conference. The first dealt with the threat of starvation caused by the exhaustion of food reserves. I believe this immediate problem will be effectively tackled. But there is also the even more important, long-term problem of increasing food production, particularly in the developing world. The developing nations themselves have the immediate and primary responsibility for this task but through lack of capital and technology they cannot tackle it alone without massive assistance from the developed world.
A resolution was passed, as the minister told us in his statement, for the setting up of a fund for agricultural development. That was introduced by some of the OPEC nations and I regard it as one of the most encouraging features of the conference. I understand a follow-up conference is to take place on November 29 under the auspices of the Secretary General of FAO, with a view to putting reality into the proposals for this fund.
Above all, the third world of the developing nations must be put in a position where it is not the recipient of hand-outs but is enabled, through expanding trade, independently to expand its own agricultural production.
World Food Conference
What am I to say about the contribution of Canada in this regard? The minister has spoken in the usual glowing and customary terms of self-praise and it is hardly necessary for me to add very much to that. Although I am a member of the opposition and inclined to be critical, I think the specific proposals of the Canadian government to expand its food aid while emergency conditions persist, to base that food aid contribution on physical terms and not on dollars, and to commit an average of one million tons of food grains annually for the next three years, were constructive proposals and gave real leadership to the conference.
I was not so satisfied with the arrangements made by the conference, supported by Canada, in respect of world food security. In my view, it would have been far better to have created a world food bank with power to deal with speculation in foodstuffs and to stabilize food prices. Instead, what we got was a plan for national stockpiles of food grains, their use to be co-ordinated by some form of international organization. This is definitely a second-best program.
Another point I wish to mention is that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) in his speech to the conference spoke of Canada responding to countries which give high priority to developing efficient food production. Naturally, we must strive for efficiency but I warn against that being the only criterion: there is the danger that if this is done, the aid will be channelled to the wealthier producers, and this may enable them to drive small producers and landless labourers in developing countries off the land and into urban slums. That situation must be guarded against.
There is another aspect where I feel the Canadian contribution was totally inadequate. This is in respect of the drive of the third world for trade policies enabling them to expand their exports and thus to finance food production in their countries. Trade, aid and food production are intimately linked. Of course, detailed trade discussions could not take place at this conference; but it is equally true, in my judgment, that the third world was right in asking that consideration be given to the general direction to be taken on this whole vital question. In my view, the Canadian response initially was almost totally negative. The minister said it was a falsehood to say that they filibustered. They may not have filibustered, but I was there and I say that the initial attitude was almost entirely negative and a filibuster would have had the same sort of effect.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
However, I give the minister some credit. Later in the conference the attitude seemed to become more flexible. Perhaps I am giving him undue credit when I say he was responsible for that. I was extremely disturbed at the initial Canadian attitude in respect of this vitally important subject. We lined up with the wealthy, developed countries and said we would not even bother talking to the developing countries about the problems they thought were important. I must admit that that attitude changed. The final resolution was a weak compro-

November 22, 1974
World Food Conference
mise, but if the minister is responsible for changing it, in fairness I give him credit for it.
I conclude my remarks by saying that I agree with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that the key to the world food problem lies primarily in the hands of the agricultural producers both in the developed and developing countries. They must be consulted, their security considered, and there must be a radical revision by the modern world of its attitude toward the importance of agriculture. Agriculture must not be subordinate to the interests of speculators or private interests which so often control markets for their own benefit. A totally new structure is required. All these matters will not be solved, as Pope Paul said, by automatic, technical solutions: fundamental human values must be taken into account. I believe that on the whole the Rome conference pointed in the right direction. It was a step forward, and with good will and hard work it can be turned into a highly significant step in the history of humanity.
I would like to add one footnote. I join the minister in his tribute to the Canadian group which was known as NGO, a non-governmental organization. I think the Canadian group made a valuable, informed and indeed intelligent, critical contribution. If they had not been there, I am sure the Canadian contribution would have been far less than it was.

subsubtopic: WORLD FOOD CONFERENCE IN ROME-REPORT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard the statement by the Minister of Agriculture and I must say his comments were not exaggerated and I believe he is right when he says that Canada had a positive participation in that conference through its expert delegates and above all the proposals that were put forward.
Canada has been one of the most responsive countries in the past few years. It can do more and the aim of the conference was to find means of sharing the planet's food resources to meet the actual needs of hungry populations. The sight of starving people is in itself difficult to bear, but when you have suffered from hunger or seen your next of kin suffer from it in your own home, it is even worse. Then, I guess, you understand better the actual situation of those starving populations deprived of any means of developing their land to produce enough food to meet their needs.
Some hon. members have sometimes accused us, without any malice I am sure, of resenting Canada's assistance program to developing countries. Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat that we favour Canada's help to developing countries, to countries whose populations are starving, but we would like to make sure that our help reaches its destination, that people who really need it are the first beneficiaries. We have been told that huge quantities of food products have been spoiled because they were stored in the wrong kind of warehouses. Our country had made an effort, but not every necessary step was taken. I don't know if that was done accidentally or on purpose, but at all events, we still have a long way to go before those products we send to starving people reach their destination. Of course Canada has huge resources of all kings and it can even produce more.

It is not only recently we have been maintaining that Canada should put its farm land to better use so as to produce sufficiently to meet the needs of the Canadian people and also help the needy countries.
I consider, Mr. Speaker, that it is a crime against humanity that thousands of farms lie abandoned and thousands of strong workers are forced into inactivity instead of working.
During the last weeks I have received numerous petitions coming from mothers in my riding asking me to press our government that our country might adopt a better food production policy. That is what I shall do at the next possible opportunity.
When my colleagues and I had the opportunity to travel in Belgium and Holland in September 1974, we witnessed that in these two countries all farm land is developed 100 per cent. There are people who understand the necessity of making use of all their production capabilities and if Canada wants to produce more efficiently, we will immediately have to adopt stronger measures to support our farmers.
It is not enough to say that we will give, that we will do our share. We must absolutely produce if we want our wishes to take on a concrete form.
Mr. Speaker, the scandalous increase in the price of chemical fertilizers will contribute to the discouragement of the farmers and I fear that 1975 production will suffer a rather shocking drop due to the fact that I have just mentioned. The horrendous increase in the cost of farm machinery is sufficient to further discourage the farmers.
In conclusion, I would like to say that if we want to, we can, and that should be the slogan of this Parliament. It is good to have the best of intentions, but acting efficiently is even better.
Besides producing, we should adopt a system insuring distribution even onto the tables of those who are in need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I rise to propose a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the renewed representations made to most members of the House, not only in person over the past few weeks but also by hundreds of telegrams and letters, urging the House to examine the abortion laws now freely in existence in this country, and in view of the fact that this is a matter dealing with life itself, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis):
That the government be instructed to form forthwith a committee comprised of members of this House to thoroughly investigate this entire area affording such organizations as the Alliance for Life and others, in fact, all segments of our society, the opportunity to express their views on a matter involving the very lives of thousands of unborn children,

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF ABORTION PROVISION TO COMMITTEE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Order, please. The House has heard the terms of the motion. With due respect I would call the hon. member's attention to the provisions of Standing Order 43 which read as follows:
A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity ...

November 22, 1974
Representation Act, 1974
The Chair can only assume that the use of the word "urgent" and in addition the words "pressing necessity" makes specific reference to the fact that a motion be not only important, as the subject matter of the motion is, but have an element of immediacy, of "urgent and pressing necessity". I am afraid, with due respect to the hon. member, that I am not able to see that the matter, while important, has any more urgency today than it did in the last parliament or that it will have in future parliaments. It is a matter of prominent and important concern to all members of the House but surely the fact of recent representations cannot take it out of the level of continuing concern and place upon it the element of urgent and pressing necessity as declared by the terms of the Standing Order. I, therefore, regret that I cannot put the motion.

subtopic: SUGAR-ATTITUDE OF CANADA TOWARDS NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT AND PRICE TO BE OFFERED

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: SUGAR-ATTITUDE OF CANADA TOWARDS NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT AND PRICE TO BE OFFERED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. As Canadian housewives and Canadians generally pay what is probably the highest price in the world for sugar as a result of Canada's inflexibility and parsimonious attitude to producing countries during the 1973 sugar talks, will the minister assure the House that Canada will now take the lead in negotiating a new sugar agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: SUGAR-ATTITUDE OF CANADA TOWARDS NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT AND PRICE TO BE OFFERED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we shall be interested in negotiating a new sugar agreement if we can find the basis for a new sugar agreement which will provide for stability of supply for consuming nations and fair prices to producing nations. So far we have not been able to find that basis.

subtopic: SUGAR-ATTITUDE OF CANADA TOWARDS NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT AND PRICE TO BE OFFERED
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In order to avoid the confusion which arose during the 1973 sugar talks concerning Canada's unwillingness to negotiate a fair price for sugar, will the minister tell the House what price Canada is now offering sugar producing countries for their sugar?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: SUGAR-ATTITUDE OF CANADA TOWARDS NEW INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT AND PRICE TO BE OFFERED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no active negotiations are going on at present. I indicated to the House that we have two preparatory groups which are ready to proceed, both with respect to questions concerning stability of supply and the question of price. We shall be prepared to sit down with producing nations as soon as they indicate to us that they are prepared to meet, as well. I should point out also that Canada is not alone in wishing to take part in these negotiations. Canada is but one of a number of consuming nations. A large number of under-developed countries are consuming nations and net importers of sugar rather than net exporters. They, too, have very important views on the price of sugar.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Considering that 100,000 automotive workers in the United States have received word that they will be laid off immediately or very soon, and, consequently, as the industry has announced that it will lay off workers in Windsor, St. Thomas, Ajax and Oshawa, and that more lay-offs will follow in Canada, what has the minister's department done in terms of forecasting future lay-offs? Further, what plans has the department made in order to deal with these forthcoming, serious lay-offs in this industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILES-FUTURE EFFECT ON CANADIAN AUTO AND RELATED INDUSTRIES OF LAY-OFFS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have the matter under continuing study. I indicated that I participated recently in a number of meetings with members of the industry. As for the second part of the question, let me refer the hon. member to the statement made by the President of the United Auto Workers of America. He pointed out that Canadian economic policy seems to be much better designed to maintain a buoyant climate for the automobile industry in this country than is the case in his country.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILES-FUTURE EFFECT ON CANADIAN AUTO AND RELATED INDUSTRIES OF LAY-OFFS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The president of the UAW was comparing what they have down there with what we have, and I suppose in that context his recommendation was not bad. I do not want to be frivolous, although the minister has tried to suggest this is not a serious matter, as he usually does. May I ask the minister this: As it is estimated that one job in six or seven in Canada is related directly or indirectly to the automotive industry, what studies has the minister's department undertaken into the indirect effects of United States lay-offs which will affect employment not only in southern Ontario, but everywhere from St. John's to Vancouver? Has the minister's department determined what other industries will be affected if the inevitable lay-offs in the automotive industry take place? What has the minister done to counter the indirect effects?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: AUTOMOBILES-FUTURE EFFECT ON CANADIAN AUTO AND RELATED INDUSTRIES OF LAY-OFFS IN UNITED STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we do not accept the premise of the hon. member's question. We do not think there will be the large number of lay-offs to which he refers. I have said to him that we expect lay-offs of a short and periodic nature from time to time, as a result of the situation in the United States. Indeed, at present we are witnessing a number of lay-offs in companies supplying parts to U.S. automobile manufacturers but, according to indications, these will be of a relatively short duration. I do not anticipate, at present, massive lay-offs in Canada such as have taken place in the United States, or such as the premise or preamble to the hon. member's question suggest.

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-SUGGESTED REDUCTION OF DIFFERENTIAL IN PRICE BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a final supplementary question. Considering that consumers in Canada, automotive workers in Canada and in the United States and the American government have all been pressing the government of Canada to bring down the price of automobiles in Canada, which would be a method miles ahead of any other for generating employment in the industry in Canada, and considering that on the assembly line in Oshawa this morning two identical cars were produced, one to go the United States and one to be sold in Canada for $1,000 more than is charged in the United States for that car, the price differential being considerably greater than the 7 per cent or 8 per cent differential the minister has talked about, when is the minister finally going to do something to reduce the price differences in this industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-SUGGESTED REDUCTION OF DIFFERENTIAL IN PRICE BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

I remind the hon. member that import today account for close to 15 per cent of the total market, whereas two years

November 22, 1974
Oral Questions
ago they accounted for close to 25 per cent. That is a reflection of the narrowing of the price difference.

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-SUGGESTED REDUCTION OF DIFFERENTIAL IN PRICE BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. In light of the fact that conflict of interest guidelines for civil servants require them to disclose apparent conflicts of interest while there is no requirement of disclosure on the part of cabinet ministers, can the Prime Minister tell the House why his government is insisting on more stringent rules governing the conduct of civil servants than those governing their political superiors?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may have misunderstood the purport of the question, but there are, of course, guidelines requiring ministers to disclose conflicts of interest.

subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Apparently the Prime Minister forgets the statement he made to the House last year in which he said cabinet ministers could put their holdings in so called blind or frozen trusts, as did the Prime Minister. Is it the

policy of the government to allow civil servants to place their holdings in frozen trust, which remain secret from everyone except the individuals involved and their trustees at the same time as they are able to influence public policy that may directly enhance their holdings, as is the case with cabinet ministers?

subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is not the case with cabinet ministers nor will it be the case with civil servants who each have to report to the minister on the action they have taken to eradicate or eliminate any conflict of interest.

speechtext: The hon. member is obviously making a series of representations on what he thinks the conflict of interest guidelines should be. We have laid the guidelines before the House.

subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: They are just a smoke screen.

subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: We are prepared to defend them. If members opposite feel they do not go far enough, they in conscience can take their own action, as did the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.

subtopic: DIFFERENCE BETWEEN GUIDELINES FOR CABINET MINISTERS AND CIVIL SERVANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speechtext:

November 22, 1974

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should first like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on what I sincerely believe is the best economic budget we have ever had in that it is reasonable, sensible and of benefit to all Canadians. Certainly, the reductions in income tax will be of benefit to all Canadians, as will the reduction in the tax on building materials which amounts to a saving of $650 on the purchase of a home. I should also like to refer to the $500 grant to those purchasing new, moderately priced homes within the next year. I think this provision should have gone a little further and made the grant available to individuals purchasing their first home who, because of limited income, must of necessity purchase an older home. I think they, too, should have the benefit of this $500 grant.
I am receiving a great many representations from people on low incomes who want to purchase a home for the first time but can only afford an older home. Surely they should be given some consideration by the government in respect of this proposed grant. To this end, I hope the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the cabinet as a whole will give consideration to this matter and will come up with a proposal as soon as possible.
I have congratulated the minister. It is not often that I rise and give out congratulations, but today I will speak of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) who represents Winnipeg South. I would be in favour of main-

November 22, 1974

taining the number of armed forces personnel at the target of approximately 82,500. I know the minister is making representations to the cabinet to this end, and also to obtain a sufficiently large budget to provide our armed forces with the proper, necessary equipment for training, for peacekeeping activities, for NORAD and NATO, for aid to civilian authorities, and so on. I believe the Minister of National Defence has done a tremendous job in making these representations to the cabinet. The minister has also done a great job in bringing industry to western Canada, at the risk, in many instances, of being criticized. He has put his job on the line and his head on the block. The Minister of National Defence is very sincere in what he is doing; and with reference to pork-barrelling in certain areas, there is certainly less of it in western Canada, especially in Manitoba and Winnipeg.
I would like to refer to some things the minister might have done. With regard to the 12,697 pairs of snowshoes which are being purchased in Ontario at a cost of over $100,000 more than if they were purchased in Winnipeg at the retail price, I compliment the Winnipeg Free Press for bringing this matter to the attention of the public. I am certain that the fact they were not bought in western Canada is not the fault of the minister. I shall now refer to some things that the minister has done to the benefit of western Canada-and there is no doubt that the west needs a lot more help. Since we have been debating the budget, the opposition have made frequent references to the fact that very few Liberal members are from western Canada. It was said yesterday by opposition members- and I listened very carefully-that this government does not pay enough attention to western Canadians and this is the reason so few Liberals represent that part of the country.
I say to you, Madam Speaker, that the voice of the Minister of National Defence and the voice of all western Canadians is clearly heard and listened to. I suggest that without doubt western Canada would receive its fair share even if there were no Conservatives representing it in this House nor, for that matter, any Liberals. As I have said, there are very few of us; however, I think the number is unimportant. What has the Minister of National Defence done to benefit western Canada? Let me give a few examples. The Arctic trading centre in northern Manitoba at Churchill means that the expenditures of the Canadian forces personnel living permanently in Churchill, in addition to the expenditures of hundreds of personnel sent there from time to time for training, will help to strengthen the economy of northern Manitoba. This trading centre was opened in response to requests from the town of Churchill and the people living in the area, as well as requests from members on this side of the House.
Throughout the province there was during the past year a substantially increased expenditure by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Within the last year, 41 incentive grants have been made to encourage small business activities. More than 1,450 jobs have been created in Manitoba as a result of federal government grants. I am not referring to the year 1974 but, rather, to the period ending December, 1973. For example, there was the decision to build a defence research establishment in Winnipeg, another project which was brought to Winnipeg by the Minister of National Defence. This will mean more
The Budget-Mr. J.-P. Guay
jobs for university graduates in Manitoba because the variety of skills and trades related to this research project will provide more employment. Although there are seven defence research establishments throughout Canada, employing more than 2,000 people, there has never been such an establishment in Manitoba throughout the 107 years of Canada's history. This is also to the credit of the minister from the province of Manitoba.
With regard to protection of the north, increased activity and interest in the north will be created by the decision made to have Canadian naval crews undertake some of their training at Hudson Bay and Manitoba's port of Churchill. I am glad to be a member of parliament from that area. Canada is a three-ocean country and Canadian sailors should be as familiar with Arctic waters as they are with the Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. The Minister of National Defence can be credited with establishing the training base in the northern port of Churchill.
The minister has done many other things to benefit western Canada, Manitoba in particular. To name but a few more, there is the Boeing aircraft plant in Manitoba, the fresh water research institute at the university of Manitoba, built at a cost of some $8 million, the new federal building on Main Street and major renovations at Lower Fort Garry. Let me also point out that part of the Royal Canadian Mint was moved to Winnipeg, where all coins in circulation in Canada will be minted. These are certainly assets for western Canadians and we thank the minister for them. He made an all-out effort to show Canadians that no matter whether they support this government or not, they are not forgotten. The mint in Winnipeg will also be minting coins for many other countries. [Translation]
In addition, Madam Speaker, I would like to put on record in Hansard the various subventions my constituency and particularly the great number of French Canadians who live in it, have received. I am referring to the subventions allocated to the official languages program in the constituency of Saint-Boniface, from 1969 to 1974.
Madam Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock, when the House took recess, I was just starting to enumerate the subsidies to language training in my riding of Saint-Boniface. As you know, the city of Saint-Boniface itself, and not the riding, has a population of 50,000, although the two other cities in my riding, Transcona and St. Vital have a population of respectively about 26,000 and 39,000. Saint-Boniface, has the most important group of French Canadians in the west, and that is where we got subsidies under the terms of the language program.

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. J.-P. Guay
I should like to take this opportunity to put them on record. Very briefly, I will say that the SFM received, from 1969 to 1974, $562,000 for Social animation, $120,000 for support, $29,340 for publicity and $81,930 for support and activities. The Cercle Moliere received $6,500 for publicity, and $99,300 for support and activities. As you know, Cercle Moliere is well known through Canada. The choir "Les Intrepides" got $7,250 for broadcasting and $7,300 for its operations. The "100 Nons" received $5,950 for broadcasting and $35,050 for operations. The Saint-Boniface cultural Centre received $150,000 for support and administration for the period 1969 to 1973. This is a federal-provincial program. Furthermore, the cultural centre also received another $75,000 in 1973 for operations and activities.
Another organization sponsored by SFM, "Manico-pains", received $2,000 for operations, "Melo-Mani". $15,000 the "Gais Manitobains", $6,320 also for operations and the "Mini-franglais", $10,000 for operations and rapprochement which gives a total of $1,213,540 and this does not include grants under Local Initiatives Programs. And there are many other things I am not talking about.
I would like to add that the Pedagogical Institute at St. Boniface College, which is located in a new building, received, once again with the provincial government's help, $1 million in 1972-73 towards the construction and operation of this building and another $95,000 for operations, which makes up 25 per cent of the cost, the balance being paid by the provincial government. The library of this college also received another grant of $25,000.
Mr. Speaker, I am mentioning these things because I believe it is important to get them on the record not only for the organizations which received these amounts but also that other people in my riding might know what is happening.
I would also like to mention the fact that insofar as the Secretary of State is concerned, for the year 1974-75 ending March 31, franco-manitoban SFM expenses will total about $301,800. That means that the cultural centre will receive, for 1974-75, a share of $100,000, social animation, $107,000, French-English relationships, $21,800, youth, $18,000, broadcasting, $25,000, special projects, $10,000 and I am not mentioning other grants totalling $20,000.
I thought those things deserved to be mentioned along with the others.
I would also like to mention federal participation of up to 90 per cent towards construction of senior citizens' housing. As you are aware, these are arrangements between the federal government and the provincial government, under which the federal government always lends 90 per cent of the amounts required to build these houses. We have the same situation with other programs we set up with the province. The people who live in those buildings are inclined to believe that it is the provincial government that gives those things to them, and not the federal government. I think we must stress our participation in these programs and openly tell the aged that the federal government lends 90 per cent of the amounts, that it set up the program New Horizons for the Aged and that it deserves credit for that.
(Mr Guay (St. Boniface).]
I submit that the federal government is not being given enough credit for programs resulting in the building of homes including those for senior citizens. The people of Canada ought to know that we, the federal government, through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation make available 90 per cent of the funds in this area. By far the greatest proportion of the cost of these homes is borne by the federal government through grants and other payments, and not by provincial governments. Of course, the federal government has provided substantially increased financial assistance for housing of all kinds, including low-cost housing, senior citizens' homes, and so on. For example, in one year the federal government provided $94 million for housing programs in Manitoba. These facts are well worth noting.
I see that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) is present. What I am about to mention I think will interest him. I am referring to an article, by Frances Russell, carried in the Winnipeg Free Press of November 18 last. The headline is, "Fired on from all sides". The article refers to the efforts of the Minister of National Defence to have Air Canada establish an overhaul base in Winnipeg. It speaks of Air Canada building its own $15 million hangar to be used for overhaul work of its own and other aircraft. The target was the creation of 800 jobs. I have spoken to the Minister of National Defence about this, and I will say that when he makes a promise he always fulfils it. I have discussed the matter with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and have been assured that this promise will be fulfilled. Actually, the Prime Minister made the statement on behalf of the Minister of National Defence. So I wish to reassure my constituents that this promise will be carried out and it will be of significant benefit to all Manitobans.
I now refer to my own bill, Bill C-139, which was presented in the previous parliament. The same proposal is now before this House but the number of the bill has been changed. I believe that members on all sides supported my previous bill and I hope they will wholeheartedly support my present proposal. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) and his officials support my proposal. I believe it would have been carried if the election had not intervened. Of course, what is proposed can be carried out in many different ways. Although the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) established the Hall commission to look into various aspects of railway workers' pensions, and although that commission is doing a good job and I see nothing wrong with it, I believe its establishment was a holding tactic because it will be a long time before the commission makes its recommendations.
That is why I have brought forward my own proposal. The government may consider the advisability of implementing it, or of doing the same thing through order in council so that railroad workers will not remain orphans, as they now are, and will be given the same benefits as are accorded to employees of other Crown corporations such as Air Canada. The employees of other Crown corporations have available to them superior pensions. I believe railway workers and railroad pensioners should be given pension benefits at least as good as those given to
November 22, 1974

employees of other government agencies. There should be parity of pensions. I believe my solution would not cost the government any more money than it is already supplying to the CNR. The time has come for all employees in the public service and in Crown corporations to be treated alike.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is known for his courage in defending people of his constituency. The remarks he made today show that he has courage in defending the minister from Manitoba. That minister needs all the defence he can get because, when the chips are down, if he cannot fulfil what he has promised he must resign from the cabinet. I hope the hon. member for St. Boniface will be on his side when that fight takes place.
Ordinarily, budget speeches try to deal with subjects which the House should face. But the present speech does not face the facts of life; it does not really deal with international monetary affairs. The entire world, including Canada, is wondering whether western nations are not plunging headlong into another ten-year depression. One would expect the budget to tell us how the government plans to head off a depression in this country, but it does no such thing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) does not seem to be aware that there are no models, no precedents to follow in the current situation. Domestic monetary and fiscal policies in Canada are still based on the concepts of the 1930s, on the concepts of Lord Keynes. Those concepts are obsolete. For example, we face shortages of internationally-traded commodities.
If we were doing our duty in this House, this debate would be centred on the necessity to develop models to grapple with the new situations which have arisen. This budget is, in a narrow sense, simply the old establishment bunch handing out a few goodies here and there. When one adds it all up, it means that you take $2 billion from the suckers-the taxpayers-because of growing inflation, and hand them back a quarter of it. Instead of dealing with the problem of inflation, particularly with regard to trade, we find our country aligning itself with resource-deficient nations of the world, especially those within GATT. We see them turning down all the efforts of the newly-developing nations to organize themselves and get a fair price for their products. We take the side of the fat-cats in a walled city handing out a few crumbs at the gates.
I could go on listing all the things a budget debate should include, but they would have to take second place to the real issue of this budget. The real issue is that this government is, unilaterally, changing the constitution of Canada. By unilateral action it is ignoring the efforts of many people over the past 20 years to find a way of bringing the constitution home and finding a way to amend it by consultation with all Canadians. The government is plunging ahead on a unilateral course that can only be described as a declaration of open war on the provinces of this country.
This is a federal state. This federal state is unique. There are not many federal states in the world and the one
The Budget-Hon. A. Hamilton
we have is unique because it seems to be working better than any other federal state. I do not intend to make a long analysis of the federal system of the United States, Malaysia, Australia or any other country that has the system. I am simply saying ours has worked reasonably well for 107 years. It is an example to the world that people of different regions and different ethnic backgrounds can get along together.
This situation is being challenged. The excuse for the challenge is that there is supposed to be a shortage of oil and gas in the world. When the parliament of 1972 met, on behalf of the official opposition and with the support of the NDP I proposed to the resource minister of this country that because the world shortage of certain resource commodities, particularly energy, offered Canada one of the greatest opportunities in its history, we should develop an industrial strategy that would bring industry here on a comparative advantage basis. I proposed that all parties should pull together and help to develop not only a national energy policy but a national resource policy, and from that an industrial strategy with all the nations of the world, as a result of which everybody would benefit.
I thought that offer was accepted. We were told to wait until July, when the government would bring out its two-volume report on energy. We were told, on that basis, that we could have consultations with industry, with the provinces and the various parties in parliament, and we would evolve such a policy. However, all that fell apart on September 4, 1973, with the panic actions of the government trying to convince Canadians that the Liberal Party was the party for the consumers. The only thing of substance they had to offer was a voluntary agreement to keep the price of oil at $4 a barrel. Later that month the government brought in the export tax. They said that half of the tax would go to the producing province and half to the federal government. In November they brought on the phony oil crisis. Here were we, a nation surplus in oil, being told we must tighten our belts in order to survive. The minister said we would be short 200,000 barrels a day. I said at that time it was a shocking revelation that would increase tensions in our federal system.
The minister was so desperate in trying to make himself the Grinch who stole Christmas that he even advised Canadians to sleep two in a bed and pull down the blinds. That is how scared he wanted to make the Canadian people. In my innocence, I thought we always slept two in a bed and always pulled down the blinds. That was a phony crisis.
What was the position of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition during this period? One, consultation with the owners of these resources so they would work in co-operation for the national good. Two, to give a cushion to consumers so they would not be harmed by the rapid rise in oil and gas prices. Three, to work on a program of staging price increases that would be fair to consumers and to producers, and in harmony with the facts of economic life. Since all this staging and cushioning would be carried out as a subsidy from producing provinces, we asked that there be a quid pro quo for the producing producer. We asked the government to accept the fact that the provinces are now subsidizing us at the rate of $3 billion a year, and

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Hon. A. Hamilton
we should see that they got something in return so they would not mind continuing the generosity.
All parties supported a one-price system, (a) to help individuals, and (b) to bring industry into this country because we can produce things more cheaply with our great reserves of energy. Finally, after a lot of pressure the government gave in: they held a conference of ministers in January and a conference of first ministers in March, 1974.
In this House all parties said, after the wild panic of the fall, that statesmanship had been restored to Canada. We congratulated everybody for being able, after consultation, to bring us together. However, within hours of that agreement the government introduced into this House the petroleum administration bill of last session, Bill C-18, which constituted a breach of the agreement that had been made. They broke their word to the ten governments within hours of having given it. That can be seen in the evidence given before the committee on energy, mines and resources.
In this parliament the government brought in a revised version of the petroleum administration bill: they included natural gas, which was not part of the agreement, and the oil sands, which was not part of the agreement. They broke another agreement made by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when they assured industry that if they would put a billion dollars into the tar sands the government would not impose price controls on this resource. This bill breaks this agreement of the two ministers and the Prime Minister.
As I read this petroleum administration bill I see there is no staging formula as promised in the agreement, and no terminal date. The government wants a permanent situation. There is no quid pro quo to show we are asking two provinces to subsidize every Canadian to the extent of $3 billion a year. Above all, there was no consultation. The government said, in effect, "If you do not agree, we will enforce it; we will put in our own agreement."
The budget of May 6, the parent of this one, added the coup de grace. It said in effect, "Not only are we breaking the agreement we make with you, but we are going to break the constitution; we are going to say that the property to the people in the provinces, provincial resources, is no longer protected by the British North America Act," which states that resources belong to the provinces, and that one government cannot tax another government. The federal government said, "We shall breach sections 109 and 125 of the B.N.A. Act and declare that provincial royalties on all the resources in a province are non-deductible." The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) went on to refine that doctrine. In the election campaign he said, and I paraphrase, "We accept the fact that a royalty is the constitutional property of the people of a province, being their share of ownership, but it is only constitutional if it is a little royalty. If the royalty becomes really big, it is not constitutional."
As one of my hon. friends is quick to observe, this is like saying that a female can be partially pregnant or a little pregnant. In fact, it is all or nothing. I suggest that the war on the province which started on May 6 is now the issue

which must be resolved, not only by this parliament but by the legislatures of every province in Canada as well as by the people of Canada generally. The budget of November 18 will be known as "the war on the provinces budget." Certainly, there are a few olive branches in it to industry and to the provincial governments. The government said, in effect,: "We'll reduce our share of the profits by two points and the provinces should do likewise." If the provinces match pro rata the two points which the federal government drops, the tax will have been lessened by four points. So if the provincial government is taking 60 per cent of the profits of an industry, and the federal government takes 30 per cent, adding up to 90 per cent, then on this new olive branch theory we shall be asking industry to put up with 84 per cent.
Anyone with any knowledge of the industry knows that people who put up billions of dollars to develop these resources are unlikely to be able to operate on the basis of 84 per cent if they cannot operate when 90 per cent of their profits are being taken away from them. However, I do not want to become too involved in the details of the subject because it leads us away from the main issue. The main issue is this: the federal government is determined to establish control over provincial resources; it is determined to establish a price control system on a permanent basis; it is determined to control the supply of all resources from beginning to end. I am not talking about oil alone; I am talking about every resource, including coal, hydro, asbestos and all the minerals within a province. This is open war on the provinces. Just 107 years after the constitution was written, the federal government declares its intention to control the supply and price of provincial resources, and I refer to every aspect of provincial resources, including land.
The second thing which is obvious about the budget is that the government is amending the constitution unilaterally. All the phony conferences which have been held over the years, asking for opinions, are to be disregarded. My hon. friend, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who is rarely moved to strong words, called this treachery and deceit. I endorse the language he used. It is a planned conspiracy to change the constitution and to centralize the control of resources by bureaucrats here in Ottawa.
I have been as patient as I can hope to be with the hon. member for Rosedale who holds the energy, mines and resources portfolio. I know how difficult it is to learn all the details of this involved industry. I thought in the beginning, when I was watching him two years ago, that I was just dealing with an amateur. Then I realized that in spite of all the hard work he has done to learn all the gobbledygook-in fact, he reminds me of a computer; you push the button and get the answer-and despite all the programmed answers he has been giving, he has been blundering around, rushing this way and that way. I can only describe him by recalling a situation I encountered as a young lad. A man was walking along the street with his head away out. The farmer I worked for commented: "Here's my head; my heels are coming." In the case of the minister it is, "Here's my mouth; my brains are coming."
I do not intend to go into this matter in detail, but the Prime Minister as this parliament unfolds, will be known
November 22, 1974

as the Bronfman boy. I will say no more than that. The Minister of Finance is no longer just the nice guy, regurgitating what has been fed to him; now he has demonstrated to us that he is like a willow tree that bends in the wind in order to stay in the cabinet. He knows enough about federal systems around the world to understand the need for constant consultation. When the powers of one jurisdiction conflict with those of another, or when they overlap, there must be consultation if the system is to survive. That is why I declare this budget to be a war on the provinces. It is out to destroy the constitution and to set up centralized power. The government is choosing the course of confrontation with the ten provinces rather than the traditional approach through consultation.
My mind goes back to the years of the government led by my right hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). I remember the then minister of labour, Michael Starr, when putting together a winter works program which was clearly outside the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, saying to the municipalities, "This is how we will help you. If you want us to help you, first you must get permission from your province." No province refused the municipalities. In this way thousands of people were employed during those years of unemployment.
I can recall the same minister's work in the field of education, which is entirely outside the jurisdiction of this parliament. He went to the provincial ministers of education setting out details of the manner in which he was ready to co-operate if permission was obtained from their provinces, and we were the first government which really helped in the educational field. Take the roads to resources program: the federal government has nothing to do with building roads in the provinces, yet those roads were built with provincial consent. The ARDA program affected an area almost entirely within provincial jurisdiction, but every province accepted it. I remember the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), then minister of resources, setting up the machinery to bring an important consultative group into being; he was the minister who established the council of resource ministers, a technique for constant consultation.
I could go on and on, but I think I have made my point. All I can say is that the battle is joined. British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan will be fighting. Soon, Ontario and Quebec will join them. Hon. members have read the words of an ex-minister of the Crown, Mr. Kierans.Even that great centralizer, Mr. Lynch, believes in consultation now. I know the provinces will unite. They have to unite. Instead of being a confrontation between one big boy and one or two little boys, it will be a contest between one big boy and a lot of others. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have had the opportunity to make these comments. On another occasion I look forward to making some suggestions for dealing with this situation which I trust will be interesting to hon. members.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to take part in the budget debate, because until now very few speeches have dealt with the budget proper. I believe an attempt is made
The Budget-Mr. Chretien
to divert attention by introducing the problem of federal-provincial relations on the resource issue. I believe the budget has been extremely well received, since it includes provision by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for the transfer to the taxpayer, under various forms, of almost $800 million to help increase its purchasing power and allow him to face the current situation.
I would like to say a few words in this resource debate, because it is apparently suggested the federal government wants to take over resources. It is a fact that resources are under provincial jurisdiction, and we are fully aware of and in total agreement with that fact. Interprovincial and international trade however is the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government acted to fulfill its responsibility to make sure the development of resources benefit all Canadians. If anyone suggests the Minister of Finance and this government will not negotiate I would invite him to read the budget speech. The Minister of Finance made provision in his budget, following representations by provinces, for a partial withdrawal on the propositions put forward in April. But I hope the provinces will also understand their responsibilities. We agree that the oil industry, because of present difficulties, needs some extra liquidities at this time to keep on with its exploration work. We therefore hope the provinces will do as much as does the federal government to accommodate the industry, and this in my opinion will solve the problem. Actually, the province of Alberta wants to try to take the opportunity provided by the Minister of Finance who stepped back to give more cash flow to the oil industry. Alberta would like to take one more bite in revenues from-

speechtext: I am very pleased to speak about this matter, but not as a Quebecker. I am speaking as a man.
