speechtext: You do not know anything about the oil industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know everyone regards me as an easterner, but my grandparents on my mother's side lived in Alberta and I know that when times were tough for them they were very happy to have some help from the federal government in order to survive. I know that, not because I was told but because it is part of our family history. This is why we have confederation. I do not like hon. members not looking at both sides of the argument.
We see, in Canada, socialists in Saskatchewan trying to set up Crown corporations to isolate the resource industry from federal taxation. I do not accept that kind of socialism which does not spread wealth across the land. When hon. members rise in the House and talk about the poor, they should consider this particular aspect and then tell the government of Saskatchewan not to use this kind of

scheme to hide profitable provincial industries from the tax collector of Canada.
I was not prepared to speak about this topic, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is well able to defend himself. He made a very good speech, and I am glad to see him back in the House. I am sure the government of Alberta will start to think things over. We have moved in the right direction. There were many meetings between the two levels of government, and the budget is a move in the right direction. In the tax field we have moved back to make some money available to industry; and if the government of Alberta wants to find the liquidity needed for industry in the province to expand, they should do likewise.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You took that away in May; don't forget that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is how I see the problem, and I always like to speak my mind. That is why I think I should give hon. members a break, because apparently when I speak my mind they get excited. I will take my text and just read it in the traditional way. I have always felt that this issue should not be only one-sided, and I hope members will understand that.
The last time I spoke at length about government expenditures was when the House was in committee of the whole considering the first supplementary estimates for this year. At that time I tried, in the briefest possible terms, to explain the content of government expenditures as they had developed and as reflected in the estimates presented to the House up to that time. That very day I was given some encouragement to believe that an understanding about the nature of government expenditures had begun to penetrate the understanding of a number of members opposite because the comments made were, in the main, constructive and sensible. Unfortunately, the comments of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) were an exception. He proceeded to classify the total budget expenditure indiscriminately as a rip-off and spoke of expenditures as being out of control, playing again the same old theme he has played on so many occasions over the years.
However, my message must have done some good because I note that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), in his remarks on the budget earlier this week, generally spared us the usual expressions of horror about government expenditures. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), when he followed and spoke on behalf of his party, was similarly restrained. I am not in the least accepting what they said about the subjects they raised, hut at least we heard no easy generalizations about waste, extravagance and about cutting expenditures. Therefore, I am encouraged that the attempts I have made, and those of my predecessor in this ministry, to inform our colleagues opposite about the composition of government expenditures are beginning to be successful.
This morning I tabled a second set of supplementary estimates for the year. I want now to anticipate some of the questions that may arise, and to place the estimates figures in clear relationship with the figures used by the
November 22, 1974

Minister of Finance in his budget. This second set of supplementary estimates is very large-$1,749 million. They are larger than any previous supplementaries for one circumstances which also dominated the budget speech: this circumstance is, of course, inflation.
Almost three-quarters of the supplementaries, that is $1,200 million, are related in some way to inflationary pressures either in the way of new costs created by inflation or in the way of increased expenditures the government has decided upon to soften the impact of inflation for some groups of Canadians. These latter expenditures should be recognized as a continuation of the government's well established policy of selective countermeasures, where we see they are most called for, to deflect the full brunt of the very real distress that rapidly increasing prices can cause.
Let me give three or four examples. The government has doubled the provisions made for subsidies on manufacturing milk and cream from the $125 million in the main estimates. These supplementaries add another $125 million. In the same item in the estimates, which takes the form of a payment into the agricultural stabilization account, there is also included the money needed for the premium quality beef program which operated until August, 1974, and has now been replaced by a price stabilization program. There are $202 million in additional payments to the provinces under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act attributable to increased tax yields in certain provinces, which are in turn attributable in great part to the effects of inflation.
There is an item of $118 million to compensate the railways for their having frozen the level of freight rates throughout this year. The additional contributions to the provinces under shared-cost programs affecting hospital insurance and university education total $125 million because hospitals and universities have higher costs to meet. We have no control over those costs; they just send us the bill.
I wonder, in passing, if hon. members opposite would stop their tirade about federal-provincial relations long enough to take note of the fact that much of the federal government's expenditure at this time, and at any time, is made up of payments to the provinces. They should stop to see how well this fact squares with their charges of centralization and betrayal. One might expect even an opposition at the federal level to adopt a more responsible line.
Another portion of the supplementaries is related to economic development and supply, such as $18 million more in capital subsidies for the construction of commercial and fishing vessels and $20 million for a loan toward the completion of the heavy water plant at Glace Bay. That is the plant started by the Leader of the Opposition when he was premier of the province, and he forgets that he put some salt in the water rather than using clear water. There was also $50 million in loans to the CNR, and $19 million for hydro projects in the north by the Northern Canada Power Commission. We have, as well, additional social measures including $30 million for Indian economic development and other needs of our Indian and Innuit population, and about $90 million related to the Local Initiatives Program for this and the past season.
The Budget-Mr. O'Sullivan

Up till now, Mr. Speaker, government estimates total $24,516 million. In view of the usual difference in expenditures-indeed, experience has shown that about 2 per cent of all the credits are not used-I expect that real expenditures as concerns estimates submitted up till now will total about $23.9 billion.
The Minister of Finance set the total expenses to be incurred during this fiscal year at $24,850 million. Excluding serious unanticipated requirements, this means that we are once again expecting to submit supplementary estimates for expenditures of approximately $900 million. The largest item in these estimates will apply to oil import compensations which would be paid under the act yet to be passed by Parliament.
The Minister of Finance included a few tables in his speech of last Monday. One of these tables shows the budget expenditures for 1973-74, 1974-75 and 1975-76, that is the real expenditures for the first year, and of course expected expenditures for the other two. The figures and increased percentage from one year to the next are as follows: in 1973-74, budget expenditures amounted to $20,040 million, or an increase of 24.3 per cent over the previous year, increase which is mostly due to the new family allowances. In 1974-75, expected budget expenditures amount to $24,850 million, or an increase of 24 per cent over 1973-74. In 1975-76, Mr. Speaker, budget expenditures are expected to be $28,750 million, which means an increase of about 15 per cent over 1974-75.
In this respect, it is most important to understand that the increase is largely due to inflation and to one of the inflation related measures. I am talking about compensations for oil imports. This item alone will increase by $1 billion the expenditures of the current fiscal year over those of last year. This sum subtracted, there has been an increase of only 19 per cent between the real expenditures for 1973-74 and estimates for 1974-75.
I do not intend to keep at this at length, even though I have other notes. I just want to say in concluding that next year, we want to reduce new expenditure to a minimum. Of course, the expenditure will rise because 56 per cent of the budget is related to outlays which leave us no choice at all, such as the automatic indexation of old age security and family allowances, or equalization payments over which we have no control.
I can assure hon. members we are determined to contain the level of expenditure next year, as much as it will be possible so as not to further feed inflation and create a situation whereby government expenditures could cause additional problems for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I am glad I had this opportunity of making those few comments. I have not finished my speech because I should have liked to give an ad lib outline of my views on federal-provincial relations and the problem of provinces which make exaggerated claims on the new wealth discovered within their boundaries.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in considering the budget presented in the House
1584

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. O'Sullivan
last Monday a time honoured phrase keeps coming to mind, caveat emptor. I say so, Mr. Speaker, for upon cursory examination the budget seems to be a rather impressive piece of work. It looks good. And, when presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), with his customary style and aplomb, it sounds good. There is no doubt that it contains some worthwhile measures, but any member of parliament who has watched how this government operates cannot help but react with some concern, and caution the Canadian taxpayer to beware before buying without reservation the minister's fourth attempt at a budget.
Like the minister, I do not claim to be an economist and, like the minister, my instinctive reaction is to think of the constituents whom I am honoured to represent and to ask how this budget will affect the labourers of east Hamilton, the merchants in Ancaster, and the young couple in Stoney Creek who dream of owning their own home.
There seems little point in asking how this document will affect the farmers in Glanbrook and other parts of my riding because in this budget they seem to have been forgotten, left out in the Ottawa cold.
At the same time I share with other members of the House a responsibility to consider the impact the budget will have on Canadians everywhere, particularly upon Canadians who, like the people of Hamilton-Wentworth, still subscribe to the belief upon which this nation was founded and has prospered, who still believe that a man should get what he works for and that he should work for what he gets.
In considering this budget we must recognize that the foundations of our society have been shaken by a crippling wave of inflation. Indeed, we are now being made aware of the very real possibility of a serious recession. One might accept the design of this expansionary budget to prevent already high levels of unemployment from reaching disastrous proportions. However, if the government lays claim to virtues in combating unemployment, it must also accept the blame for contributing to it.
Thousands of jobs go begging in Hamilton today, including high paying jobs at the steel companies. Among the reasons are government policies which discourage incentive and make it more inviting for some simply not to work. The cost to Canadians of the Unemployment Insurance Commission remains at over $2 billion, yet this government still refuses to have an independent inquiry to clear up the mess and clear away the waste. One can only conclude that the government is indifferent to such waste, or it is afraid of an inquiry.
It would appear that the minister continues to embrace the outdated tradeoff between unemployment and inflation. Surely this simplistic concept has been discredited, and it is no longer reasonable to ask Canadians to accept higher and higher rates of inflation in another attempt by the minister to keep unemployment at levels the government considers tolerable.
In an economy as complex as ours it becomes imperative that the twin scourges of unemployment and inflation be attacked jointly and decisively. Anything less is an admission of the inability of the government to cope with the problems it was given a mandate to solve.

We of the Progressive Conservative Party have long called for cuts in the tax bills of Canadians, made possible chiefly through a re-alignment of federal spending priorities and elimination of government waste. And so, while we welcome the minister's announcement of a cut, however small, in personal income tax, we view with alarm the fact that the federal government's budget continues to increase at alarming rates and itself feeds inflation.
Canadians are becoming even more concerned at the tremendous size and expense of government without experiencing any commensurate tangible benefits. In welcoming the small cut in taxes the Canadian taxpayer should not lose sight of the fact that what he is receiving is not a gift but just a bit more of the money he worked so hard to earn.
It is analagous to the Minister of Finance taking a $10 bill which has fallen from someone's pocket, then turning around and giving back $2-apparently out of the goodness of his heart. The poor luck fellow would think he had just met a very kind and generous man, until he discovered that he was missing his $10. Then he would realize he had just met Canada's finance minister.
Clearly these tax cuts could have been more meaningful if only the government would practice in its own spending the kind of restraint it asks of workers in setting wage demands, and of companies in setting their prices. One need only go through the spending estimates of almost every government department to find examples of duplication and waste. While there have been some very worthwhile projects, we still hear examples of thousands of tax dollars going to highly questionable LIP and OFY projects. One must not forget the Company of Young Canadians, even though the government would like to, Mr. Speaker. Recently we learned that External Affairs granted over $300,000 to a terrorist group in Africa. One wonders, in view of Canada's shameful abstention at the United Nations, whether similar aid will soon be granted to the murderous Palestinian Liberation Organization.
The government could also be more responsible in deciding where money should be spent. We recently heard the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) admit that our armed forces can no longer afford to patrol Canada's north to watch for Soviet incursion into our territory. The government continually downgrades our involvement in NATO, using budgetary restraints as an excuse. Canadians would not begrudge the careful use of their tax dollars to ensure the morale of our armed forces, to protect Canada's sovereignty, and to honour our commitments to international peace and freedom.
In this debate there has been much discussion about Canada's resources and Canada's future. I think we would all agree that, in terms of her future, Canada's greatest resource is the potential of young Canadians. If that resource is to be developed fully we must offer all young Canadians, regardless of their financial background, equality of opportunity to acquire an education and useful skills.
Although education falls within provincial jurisdiction, the federal government long ago recognized the need for it to assist in this important field. Since costs of vocational
November 22, 1974

schools, colleges and universities are increasing tremendously I would simply like to reiterate the words of another hon. member who sits in this chamber, and who said:
I hope that some day we will move toward a gradual reduction and an eventual abolition of student fees at all levels ... I am not suggesting that we should subsidize the small part of the population that may have the talent or initiative to obtain a university education. I hope that in the whole realm of technical and vocational education, as well as university education, we would move gradually toward the elimination of student fees.
I endorse those words which appear on pages 6616 and 6617 of Hansard for June 20, 1966, and were spoken by the then member for St. Lawrence-St. George. Today he sits in this House as the member for Ottawa-Carleton, and on the treasury benches as the Minister of Finance. Now that he is in a position to do so, I hope he will act upon his own worthwhile suggestion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't count on it!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an area in which the minister has taken some positive action is with regard to the housing crisis. For several years my party has called for the elimination of the 11 per cent federal tax on building materials. The minister took a step in the right direction by reducing this tax, but as the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) pointed out, the collection of a 5 per cent tax still requires as big a bureaucracy.
Additional bureaucrats will be required to administer the grants of $500 to each purchaser of a new home, so long as it is "moderately priced". In setting its standards of what constitutes moderate pricing, I would hope that the government will bear in mind the astronomical increases in housing costs in recent years, especially in southern Ontario, and I would suggest that the limit be set just slightly below the going rates to encourage developers to bring down the prices of their units to the acceptable level. Ultimately, however, I think we have to forgo such patchwork measures in favour of a wholesale review of housing financing.
As pointed out by Dr. James Johnston, an economist and publisher of the Cobourg Sentinel-Star, it is simply no longer fair to ask potential homeowners to compete for loanable funds from the same sources as giant corporations, which can meet high interest rates and even charge them against taxes. In finding a way truly to assist Canadian families in housing, we can start on the road to the desirable situation of having double income families by choice and not out of sheer economic necessity.
To this point, Mr. Speaker, my remarks have dealt with a few of the technical aspects of government economic policy. It has become a tradition to look upon a budget as some kind of a periodic report of revenue and expenditure of government. I strongly feel it should go beyond that and truly be a statement of social purpose as well.
That is why the highlight of this budget, for me, was the recognition by the Minister of Finance of Canada's obligation to do everything possible to combat the world food crisis. My concerns about this terrible and continuing tragedy were outlined when I spoke earlier this week in the debate on Bill C-10. So, at this time I simply wish to commend the minister, in a very sincere and non-partisan
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas
way, for reflecting the feelings of all of us and for undertaking a commitment to our brothers and sisters in mankind who look to us for help.
May that statement by the minister also start a tradition of making the budget a commentary on the social, as well as the financial policies of a government. We cannot separate productivity from the question of our qualify of life. We should not talk of consumption without speaking of conservation. We must not set out to create jobs without first deciding conditions of work.
We must recognize that the facts and figures side of a budget is not all that an economy is, or all that it should be. And one must remember that the gross national product measures neither our wisdom nor our courage, neither our integrity nor our compassion. So, Mr. Speaker, a budget should say more, not just about our national productivity but also about our national spirit.
I commend the Minister of Finance for the positive efforts contained in his budget. I hope he will accept my comments in the spirit with which they are offered, for although we have our differences about some of the budget provisions and other government policies, I believe he is doing his best at a most difficult time. For the sake of the people we all seek to serve, I wish him well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if I had the time I should like to discuss several aspects of this budget, which I consider is designed to help those who have too little by giving tax concessions to those who have too much.
Since I only have a limited time, however, I propose to devote myself primarily to that portion of the budget which deals with resource taxation, the repercussions of which could cause great disunity in this country. I discuss this question as one who, throughout his political life, has been a firm advocate of a strong federal government. I would go further. The New Democratic Party has consistently supported the concept of a strong federal government clothed with the power necessary to deal effectively with social and economic problems. For instance, the New Democratic Party advocated and supported a two price system for oil, and a single price across Canada, in order to protect the Canadian people against the 400 per cent increase in international oil prices.
The New Democratic Party has supported Bill C-32 which is still before the committee of the whole of this House and which will become the Petroleum Administration Act. If this bill is passed it will provide that, in the event negotiations are not successful with the provinces, the government may establish a price in Canada for all oil and gas entering into interprovincial and international trade. On November 13 and 14 I argued in this House that the federal government must have that power if we are going to deal with the problem of energy supplies in this country. I must say, however, that the budget may cause us to re-examine our position if the federal government intends to use its powers in the ruthless manner which it is now displaying.
Canada needs a strong federal government in order to cope with the many problems of this country, and nowhere is this more necessary than in the field of energy where we are faced with a crisis in the years immediately ahead.

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas
But we contend that the powers granted to the federal government should not be used to trample upon the legitimate rights of provincial governments, nor should those governments be tricked into agreements which are later repudiated.
I think the provincial governments acted in a statesmanlike manner at the First Ministers Conference which was held in Ottawa on March 27 last. On March 28 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) paid tribute to the provincial premiers in the following terms, as recorded at page
933	of Hansard. He said that we had reached:
... An agreement... which stands as a tribute to the vitality of our Canadian community ... yesterday was a great day for federalism.
The Prime Minister went on to say, as recorded at page
934	of Hansard:
The national oil agreement I have just described would surely not have been possible without the good will and deep commitment to Canada of the premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan.
I submit, Madam Speaker, that these tributes were well deserved.
What did the oil and gas producing provinces agree to do? They agreed to accept a price of $6.50 per barrel, when the Chicago price at that time was between $10 and $11 per barrel, and now it is much higher. Every barrel of oil sold in Alberta and Saskatchewan is being sold for $5 less than could be secured on the Chicago market, plus transportation. In other words, the provinces gave up over $2 billion. I am one who supported what they did. Considering the type of national emergency we faced then and which we still face, a price must be set to protect the Canadian people from exorbitant international oil prices. The provincial premiers agreed to this.
Further, they agreed to forgo the 50 per cent share of revenue from the export tax which they had received up until then. On the basis of the production of 1,200,000 barrels a day during the last 12 months, one can say that Alberta and Saskatchewan gave up some $800 million or $900 million from this source. Those were great concessions, and the Prime Minister was right in saying they were made possible only with the good will and deep commitment of the provincial governments concerned.
In return the Prime Minister committed the federal government first, to a just and reasonable price for this depleting resource; second, to assist the provinces in developing new oil resources; and, third, to help those provinces ensure alternative economic development. In order to carry out the commitment to assist the provinces in developing new oil resources the Prime Minister agreed, and so reported to this House, that the federal government would allow the oil producing provinces to set up capital funds for resource development, into which they could put their additional oil revenues, and that those funds would not be taken into consideration in determining equalization payments.
Let me put the Prime Minister's words on record. They are crystal clear. He said, as recorded at page 934 of Hansard for March 28:
The House may wish to note that Saskatchewan intends to place most of its added oil revenues in a capital fund for energy develop-

ment; Alberta proposes to handle a high proportion of its added revenues in the same manner ...
While the revenues taken into those capital funds would not be subject to equalization, the federal government will, of course, pay equalization respecting any oil revenues that go into general funds.
That was the commitment. Nobody expected that revenues which went into the general account would not be taken into consideration in determining equalization payments. But there was the clear understanding that if a province chose to set up a contingency fund, a depreciation account to enable it to replace a resource which is depleting far more rapidly than most people realize, that fund would not be taken into account when the equalization formula is computed.
What happened, Madam Speaker? In the budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) says that one third of the additional oil revenues of those two provinces combined will be considered as revenues for equalization purposes. He is to do this by estimating the total amount which will be going into general revenue. But that is not in accordance with what the Prime Minister said on March 28, as I have quoted. He said that Saskatchewan proposes to put most of its revenue into the capital account. There was no mention then of lumping both provinces together, and there was no mention of roughly one third of the total amount which comes from additional oil revenue going into general revenue because Alberta proposes to put a larger amount into general revenue. Actually, Saskatchewan has carried out its part of the understanding to the letter. It has placed all its additional oil revenue, every nickel, into a capital account for resource development, because it needs millions of dollars if it is to develop heavy oil in the Cold Lake district.
The government is breaking its commitment. It is saying to Saskatchewan, "You will be lumped together with Alberta. We estimate that roughly one third of the total additional oil revenue of both provinces is going to general revenue and therefore you will lose, under the equalization formula, $40 million a year."
I submit that either the Prime Minister misled the provinces and the House when he reported to us on March 28, or the Minister of Finance has overruled the Prime Minister. The heir apparent is now telling the king what to do. This reminds me of what Shakespeare said:
Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed,
That he is grown so great?
The provinces justifiably feel they have been tricked and betrayed. I submit, Madam Speaker, that this will not encourage federal-provincial cooperation. The west will feel that it is paying a heavy price for the majority it enabled the Liberal government to acquire in the last election.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The west does not provide the government's majority.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But it
sent back enough members to enable the government to have its majority. The old arrogance is back. We can live with that. But welching on a solemn commitment is something which the Canadian people, including many Liberal supporters, will not condone.
November 22, 1974

Further, the government has shown its appreciation to the provincial governments for their cooperation by declaring that oil, gas and mineral royalties will not be deductible for income tax purposes by the producers of these commodities. For the first time in the history of Canada the federal government has said that royalties paid to a provincial government shall no longer be deductible for income tax purposes. This is utterly absurd. Why, Madam Speaker? First, royalties paid on freehold, say by the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Hudson's Bay Company, will be deductible, but royalties paid to a provincial government will not. I know of Canadian companies which own properties in other countries. The royalties they pay to foreign governments will be deductible, but royalties paid to a provincial government in Canada will not be, Madam Speaker.
If Imperial Oil Company spends $10 million in an advertising campaign to increase the consumption of gasoline, which we ought to be conserving, it can deduct that. However, if it pays $10 million in royalties to the oil producing provinces, that is not deductible. The argument made by the Minister of Finance, and made again this afternoon by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), is that the government wants to share its resource revenues with all the people of Canada.
May I first point out that the federal government has other ways of taxing oil and gas companies. It could, if it wanted, impose an excess profits tax. On the contrary, it has reduced the tax rate and exempted the oil and gas companies from the 10 per cent surcharge. It could reduce the depreciation and depletion allowances. Instead, it has given them 100 per cent write-off for exploration and 30 per cent for development.
The sharing of oil revenues in all parts of Canada and treating everybody equally, is something which ought to be examined. I noticed a press release issued by Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan the day before yesterday. May I quote a small part of it:
If Saskatchewan levies a royalty of $1 a barrel on Imperial Oil, we receive $1. However, for every $1 of provincial income tax paid by Imperial Oil, Saskatchewan's share is less than four cents. Imperial Oil is a large company, operating across Canada, and its provincial taxes are divided among the provinces according to a formula based on its wages and sales in each province-not its oil production.
So, for every dollar of provincial tax paid by Imperial Oil, Ontario gets about 30 cents, even British Columbia gets more than six cents. And Saskatchewan gets less than four cents.
When the government talks about everybody sharing equally in the taxes from the resource'industry, it seems that the tax structure which the government has built should be subject to re-examination. Moreover, Madam Speaker, are these royalties which are declared nondeductible on non-renewable resources to apply eventual-1 ly to renewable resources? On November 20 I asked the Minister of Finance a question with regard to royalties and stumpage duties. As recorded at page 1488 of Hansard, the minister answered in part:
If, of course, stumpage dues were to be converted from a flat, classical type of royalty payment into a disguised tax, we would need to look at that as well.
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas
When is a royalty not a royalty? Answer: when the Minister of Finance says it is not a royalty. The Minister of Finance does not stop there in his bull in the china shop display of how not to get along with the provincial governments. In motion No. 9 of the ways and means resolutions we have a measure which will have the effect of either dismantling every provincial resource marketing agency or bankrupting the oil and gas companies operating in the provinces. British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan all have natural gas marketing agencies. Alberta has one handling methane and propane. The province of Saskatchewan has one handling petroleum. Let me give an example.
In the province of Saskatchewan, starting back 20 years ago, Saskatchewan Power Corporation was given authority not only to handle the production and distribution of electrical power, but also the transmission and retailing of natural gas. It buys gas from a producer at 16 cents per thousand cubic feet. It is sold to the people of Saskatchewan at no profit, as close to cost as possible.
Under the provisions of the No. 9 ways and means motion the government will have the right to say that the fair market value of that gas is not 16 cents, but 60 cents. The gas producing company will be required to pay its tax on the basis of having received 60 cents, or whatever other figure the government decides is fair market value, and not on the amount which it actually receives. In other words, what the Minister of Finance is seeking to do is to say that a provincial government cannot use a Crown corporation or marketing agency to give the people of that province the benefit of their resources at the lowest possible price. That is surely an infringement on the right of the provincial government.
The other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) said that this measure could force the provincial governments into nationalizing some of their industries. The NDP would certainly welcome that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
However, the Minister of Finance has already prepared a tactic to deal with that situation. Last Monday night at a press conference he said, and I quote:
Any province for its own ideological reasons that seeks to use this budget to nationalize industry and thereby capture revenues for themselves should think about it carefully, because then the federal Government will have to consider taxing Crown corporations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance is saying that if a provincial government, with the consent and support of the citizens of that province, wants to set up a Crown corporation so that the benefits of developing its resources

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Mclsaac
will go to the people rather than to the private sector, then the Minister of Finance and the federal government will, if they think it right, tax that Crown corporation. Does the minister propose to tax Ontario Hydro, Quebec Hydro and the government telephone companies of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta? These are the things that come to the fore.
In conclusion there is to be a meeting of the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurers on December 9 and 10. I suggest to the government that this House not deal with Bill C-32, and with the bills arising out of the ways and means resolutions, until that meeting has taken place. Until the federal government and the provincial governments have had a chance to discuss this, and until the Minister of Finance has had an opportunity to be informed as to what the effects of this budget will be, we ought not to be asked to deal with that legislation. This is a vital matter.
This Liberal government, which for decades has paraded itself as being the party that can bring national unity to our country, is taking steps at the present time that will cause more disunity than I have seen since coming to this House some 39 years ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to be taking part in this debate. It is a particular privilege to follow the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who, as he said, has 39 years experience in this House as well as in the parliament of Saskatchewan. His contribution not only to Saskatchewan but to this country is well known to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is with a great deal of pride and humility that I make my first formal contribution to this debate. I wish to take advantage of the latitude normally accorded in the budget debate to discuss some of the aspirations, feelings and concerns of the people of my constituency, Battleford-Kindersley. I want to discuss some of their areas of concern and tell hon. members something about the nature of my constituency.
It is a large area in total acreage, primarily agricultural, and varying from good grain land in the southern part to grain land, grass land and excellent cattle country in the northern part of the constituency. Surprisingly enough, over half of my constituents live not on the farms but in urban centres such as North Battleford, and Battleford where 15,000 people live, Battleford, the City of Lloydmin-ster and some of the best towns in the west, like Unity, Rosetown, Kindersley, Wilkie, Kerrobert and Macklin.
During the course of the July 8 election campaign, along with my opponents and, I am sure, most other members on both sides of this chamber, I knocked on hundreds of doors and spoke with hundreds of people. I have been active in campaigns before, Madam Speaker, but this one was different. I want to tell you in what way it was different. First, regard! '~5 of their previous voting habits, people in my part of Saskatchewan did not want an election. They saw no need to be going into an election campaign. They

had just come through a tough, long winter and it had been a wet, late spring; farm work was weeks behind. To a large extent they blamed members of the New Democratic Party, and to a lesser degree members of the Conservative Party for bringing on an election.
I would point out, though, that while they did not want an election, people were happy to speak to me as a candidate-I am sure this applied to any other candidate who knocked on their doors. I have never had a better personal response regardless of how people voted in the past. I make this point in order to demonstrate the genuine interest and concern with regard to federal issues of Canadians in my province.
They are concerned about agricultural programs and policies which may, perhaps, affect them more directly than others. They are concerned about industrial development in Saskatchewan. They are concerned about such matters as local processing of agricultural products instead of this work being done at either end of the country or somewhere in between. They are concerned about the rising cost of farming, the rising costs of doing business generally, and they are concerned about the difficulty of getting manpower, whether to help on the farm or to help in the operation of a small service station. They are annoyed to think that some individuals can, and do, quit their jobs and draw unemployment insurance benefits while farmers and small business operators work double shifts to keep their operations going.
Saskatchewan people believe in working hard. They are not enthused with programs and policies which result in people being able to get along adequately by working only when they wish, or by working very little. Like most other Canadians my constituents believe that governments, both federal and provincial, are spending too much money. Mind you, at the same time when it comes to any cutbacks they believe, as do most Canadians, that such cuts should be made somewhere else. But inflation was and continues to be the cause of deep concern to my constituents.
The phrase "western alienation" has been bandied about in western Canada, in Saskatchewan and, indeed, in this chamber during recent years. The cause of western alienation is not easy to define. Indeed the definition of the phrase varies depending on the person to whom one is speaking. It means different things to different people. In some ways it is the east versus the west theme which we have been hearing for years. Ottawa is a long way from Battleford, Kindersley and Meadow Lake, and those places are further still from Montreal and Quebec City. This in itself is part of the problem-the geography of Canada itself. I mention these concerns felt by my constituents, I mention the reactions of voters in the campaign, and I mention this feeling of western alienation in order to give some picture of the thinking of my constituents before I discuss the resource taxation measures proposed in the budget.
This week we are hearing loud screams of agony from Mr. Blakeney, leader of the NDP government in Saskatchewan. On Wednesday we heard the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) criticize the budget in this House on the ground that it threatens confederation. Well, I have an oil industry in my constituency. There is a very considerable potash industry in Saskatchewan. Though
November 22, 1974

there are no potash mines in Battleford-Kindersley, the first mine to be sunk in Saskatchewan was sunk outside Unity; it never reached the potash but the know-how gained in the course of that operation led to the success of half a dozen other mines in the province. So resources and resource taxation are important to me and to my constituents.
I believe the provinces have every right to royalties from the resource industries. On the other hand I disagree with the concept now being advanced by provinces such as Alberta and Saskatchewan under which the term "royalty" includes not only rental rates in respect of resources but every cent of the profits of resource industries. The hon. member who spoke before me referred to Saskatchewan and the stand it had taken.
Let us consider the attitude adopted by Mr. Blakeney and the NDP government of Saskatchewan. What have they done to encourage resource development in the province? Last year they introduced Bill 42 in the Saskatchewan legislature, a measure which enables the provincial government to take 100 per cent of the selling price of a barrel of oil over and above the figure of $3.60, I think it was.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The NDP members opposite applaud.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Additional profit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There were other measures passed which amounted to complete confiscation of the mineral rights of the province.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Rubbish!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not rubbish. If the temporary leader of the NDP would go to Saskatchewan he would find out for himself. That Bill No. 42 effectively killed any further development of oil, gas or potash resources in Saskatchewan. Here is the proof. In January, 1974, 17 permits were issued to drill oil wells in Saskatchewan. A year earlier, in January, 1973, 86 permits were issued. Bill 42 killed exploration in Saskatchewan long before the budget of May 6, and even longer before the budget of November 18. The NDP government in Saskatchewan made similar moves affecting the forest industry and the potash industry. The potash industry is the latest to be affected.
The most recent action taken by the provincial government effectively ended any possible hope of companies getting other than a nominal return, as decided by the NDP government, on their investment. New taxes of $87 million are projected for 1975.
But Mr. Blakeney says he still wants the 46 per cent of the money he is now spending that comes from Ottawa. Keep that coming-he wants that too. Of the $1 billion that the province budgeted for last year, over $400,000 came direct from the federal treasury. Mr. Blakeney says "Don't touch that. We still like those large equalization grants". Incidentally, in the last number of years, through federal-provincial negotiations ar J conferences, the equalization grant payable to Saskatchewan has grown from
The Budget-Mr. Mclsaac
about $10 million in 1968 to almost $150 million last year, due to revisions of the formula and developments arising from these conferences. They still demand their share of medicare and education grants, and they still take the additional federal money added to equalization a couple of years ago for school board spending in the province of Saskatchewan and seven other provinces.
So I ask hon. members opposite who have been crying about this budget threatening confederation, who is threatening the resource industry? Who is being greedy and taking high handed actions which are killing further exploration and development? I cannot accuse the province of Alberta entirely because they did not take 100 per cent of the profit, only 65 per cent. But who changed the rules in resource industry taxation? Who made the first move? Not this government.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You had to throw the second stone, did you?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who is threatening confederation? Who is bleeding the resource industries dry in the province of Saskatchewan? Again I say it is not the federal government.
I am not happy with the situation in which the resource industries find themselves-far from it, Madam Speaker. I have communities like Lloydminster, Coleville and Kind-ersley that are dependent upon a healthy oil industry. Neither am I happy with the combination of moves by both the federal and provincial governments which are resulting in shutdowns of a number of wells in that particular area. I have made representations to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) to seek a better break on the export tax on Lloydminster heavy crude, which is not exactly a choice grade of crude, and I hope that this particular issue can be resolved so that oil continues to be in production and jobs in the industry in my part of the country are filled.
I may say also, Madam Speaker, that there is a definite feeling in western Canada, and certainly in my part of Saskatchewan, that the western provinces can stand some increases in revenue for the next one or two years or so, in short, some "catch-up" time if you like, to make up for some of the slack years of the past. Therefore, I urge the federal ministers responsible for energy, mines and resources and finance to keep this thought in mind as they deal with the rapidly changing issues of energy and resources today.
I spoke earlier of some of the feelings of my constituents. They want their fair share of the good things of this country, and they do not want more than their fair share. But they consider a fair share to be something more than they have been getting during the first 100 odd years of confederation. Above all, I want to say they are still Canadians first and foremost. They want one strong Canada, not ten strong states, with a weak central government.
In this respect I regret very much the narrow tone of the remarks made yesterday in this debate by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). I think any member opposite who speaks as he did is doing his province and his country a disservice in this regard. He contributes not to Canadian unity and understanding, but

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Cossitt
instead to disunity and misunderstanding. I think there is plenty of room for honest differences of political opinion between provinces and parties, but these need not result in continuing this divisive approach of the Tories and the parochial approach of the NDP.
I think the budget represents a fair compromise by the federal government on the proposals on resource revenue put forward on May 6-the tax abatement, the 100 per cent write-off for exploration costs-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was not in the
May budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it was not, and that is what I am saying. This present budget is an improvement. The next move is up to the provinces. How far will the provinces go in pushing their demands, even at the expense of changing confederation? Which industries are next? I suspect that the NDP government of Saskatchewan will move in and take over windfall profits of farmers next. That would be a very logical move for that province to make. If the governments of the provinces continue in this direction, they will very definitely change confederation and weaken the national government in this country in so doing. I am concerned to see that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources continue negotiations and, indeed, if need be enter into further trade-offs to maintain national unity
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, this budget had the general approval of the electorate on July 8. The tax relief measures for middle and low income Canadians were approved by Canadians on July 8. One of the provisions which was very popular during the election campaign was the exclusion of the first $1,000 of interest from income tax, and many other provisions in that budget received the approval of the people at that time. I am glad to see those measures brought back with the budget, and indeed other measures that will result in tax breaks for the average Canadian citizen. When one looks at this budget and the changes in direction it has taken since the May 6 presentation, it clearly demonstrates how responsive is this government to changing circumstances.
