Without any doubt, the real bigots in Canada today are those who sit in the front benches of this government; the Prime Minister and those who follow him blindly, apparently willing politically to manipulate this country on the basis of race and language for some questionable and peculiar purposes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not very questionable

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This government, whose leader has spoken often and righteously of the need for national unity, is in reality moving along a most dangerous path that leads inevitably to the destruction of national unity, a path which the Prime Minister's predecessors from Quebec, those great men Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Louis St. Laurent, would never have followed, and a path I am certain is unacceptable to the great majority of Canadians, including those living in the province of Quebec.
In the midst of this stands that dithering dilettante, Commissioner of Official Languages, Keith Spicer, in theory a servant of parliament but in practice a tool of this government. He has consistently displayed a one-sided approach to the implementation of bilingualism, flitting about the country snickering and giggling his way from soiree to soiree, coining ridiculous phrases like "West-mount Rhodesians".
Two incidents instigated by Spicer and his office in my area of Ontario serve as examples of the reprehensible methods used by this government and its supporters in implementing bilingualism. The first occurred at Prescott, Ontario, when Spicer sent one of his investigators over the International Bridge to the United States with instructions to return immediately to Canada posing as a Frenchspeaking tourist coming home from a trip with a half empty bottle of wine in his car.
This sneaky individual with his phony story was apparently attempting to trap unilingual Canada Customs officers into errors that would incriminate them in the guise of supposedly conducting an investigation of the port's bilingual facility. This member of Spicer's staff, or perhaps I should say Spicer's gestapo, even stole a scratch pad from the office counter when the customs officers were not looking. He brought it back to Ottawa and gave it to Spicer. In due course Spicer complained to the Collector of Customs that the scratch pads being used by his staff were not bilingual.
Aside from its comic Dick Tracy aspects, this incident has a serious side. It illustrates the lengths this government is prepared to go in undermining public service morale by spying on conscientious employees, sneaking around in disreputable fashion attempting to create trouble for those who are unilingual, and all this disgraceful behaviour carried out in the name of national unity, and in the name of fairly implementing bilingualism.
This summer, just a month or two ago, at the Thousand Island Bridge at Lansdowne, Ontario, in my constituency, Guy Robitaille, Spicer's chief assistant, arrived at the border from the United States at one o'clock in the morning. Speaking perfect English he demanded to be spoken to in the French language. There was no officer on duty at
The Budget-Mr. Cossitt
that time who spoke French. Immediately he proceeded to raise a fuss and insisted that a bilingual Canada Customs officer who lived 10 miles away from the port of entry be called out of bed at one o'clock in the morning and forced to dress and drive back to work to answer questions that he had already asked in English.
Just how much is it costing taxpayers to finance these nonsensical methods of implementing bilingualism? How much is being spent on salaries to those who run around on orders from Keith Spicer playing funny little games with half empty bottles of wine? How much is being spent on language courses, not just for public servants, but for the wives of senior officials, one of whom was quoted in the press not so very long ago as saying she is learning French at government expense in order to get on better at cocktail parties?
I suggest, Madam Speaker, that the implementation of bilingualism should have a thorough examination by a committee of this House. The methods of implementation being used are staggering in cost, and it is shameful that so far they have managed to escape careful scrutiny.
If ever there was anything that clearly illustrates the need for careful scrutiny it is the statement made on the implementation of bilingualism by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) yesterday. The minister released a lot of figures but not one of those figures was the estimated total cost, and it is really not hard to understand why. It is because the estimated cost of what this government plans, added to the cost of what it has already done, is so high that the Canadian people in outrage would demand an investigation if they were given such information.
A year ago the government estimated 20,000 positions in the public service would be designated bilingual. Now the minister admits that the total has reached 53,600, and that is only so far. What will it be a year from today, and what will it be two years from now?
The minister says a further 19,000, mostly Anglophone public servants, will be required to learn a second language, but for the sake of the government's skin he wisely does not say how much the schools and teachers will cost Canadians. Without doubt, the wastage of public funds runs into the millions of dollars.
We are told those age 60 and over will not be required to become bilingual. Why age 60, which in reality is the retirement age for many? Why not age 50, or for that matter why at any age in certain specific cases? Again I think of my own constituency where several years ago this government dragooned Canada Customs officers into French language courses, only to find that they soon forgot what they learned because their jobs furnished no necessity for using a second language. The taxpayers, of course, in the meantime footed the unknown bill and, magnified all across the country, we can imagine how much it has cost.
This government has turned the implementation of bilingualism into a sacred cow, supposedly on a pedestal above the right of democratic criticism, an expensive sacred cow costing Canadian taxpayers millions of dollars a year. Why should it not be examined and why should it not be criticized? Why should there be anything wrong

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Cossitt
with pointing out gross errors and ulterior motives of this government in handling the implementation of bilingualism? Most important of all, why should one hesitate to speak out against a government whose policies are so potentially damaging and ruinous to the future of Canada?
This leads me to what I think is a very peculiar situation. When persons in French-speaking Canada rightfully and proudly point to their culture and to their heritage, when they call for preservation of their traditions, this is viewed in the eyes of those who control the government as "standing up for their rights". But when persons in English-speaking Canada rightfully and proudly point to their cultures and their heritages, and call for the preservation of their traditions, in the eyes of the government this is apparently "bigotry". What kind of nonsense is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I challenge that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister says that he challenges it. The information he has given, and the information his successor now gives, lead me not to have much faith in what he says. What kind of nonsense is it? For what purposes does this government attempt to con all those Canadians whose ancestry is British, German, Dutch, American, Italian, or whatever, into believing that they are bigots and persons against national unity if they so much as utter a peep in support of the contributions made by their backgrounds and traditions to the development of Canada?
I often wonder if the Prime Minister realizes that he would not be sitting in this Canadian House of Commons if it were not for the fact that there was previously a British House of Commons that made all this possible. Perhaps the attitude of the Prime Minister on this subject is accounted for by his obvious disdain and impatience for parliament and the democratic process.
Since this government assumed office there has been a steady attempt to erode our democratic processes and to downgrade and ultimately destroy many traditions on which the institutions of this country are founded.
One needs only to remember that the Prime Minister once declared that members of the opposition were a "bunch of nobodies". What a demonstration of appreciation that was for the democratic process! One needs only to remember that the Prime Minister once told a group of working people outside this building to go and eat dung when all they were doing was exercising their democratic right to protest. What an understanding he displayed of our traditional freedom to dissent!
One needs only to remember that supreme act of hypocrisy after the government's near defeat in 1972 when the Prime Minister, who had long turned his back on the British connection, suddenly in desperation rushed off to London for tea at Buckingham Palace in an attempt to save his political skin.
For years this government has neglected our NATO friends while the Prime Minister did such things as tiptoe through the Orient to sit at the feet of Chairman Mao. Today this government still neglects our friends in Europe, despite the attempt to make it look otherwise by

the Prime Minister's recent unimpressive and not very successful afterthought visit to Brussels.
Not long ago Ivan Head, that strange ogre of the Prime Minister's office, spoke of our "new left wing foreign policy" in a move that was an all too obvious flying of a kite to see how far they could go and get away with it. But the reaction showed that there are more people than they realized in this country who know what is going on. The Prime Minister quickly pulled in his horns, reverted to his role of Prince Charming, and declared that it was all some kind of misunderstanding or misinterpretation. In other words, it is a case of holding up the con game for a while until no one is looking and then moving quickly forward with a new episode of legerdemain.
When it comes to government sleight of hand, there is no better example than its attempt sneakily to change the capital of this country. If it is government policy to change the capital from Ottawa to Ottawa-Hull, then why does the government not honestly admit it and propose an amendment to the British North America Act? But no, instead it follows the course of a sneak. Its illegal approach to this matter was clearly revealed several months ago in one of its own publications entitled "Canada's New Capital". I will quote a few words from this pamphlet:
Ottawa is the capital of Canada. Right? Wrong. It used to be that staid, musty old Ottawa was known as the nation's capital. Technically, it still is. But let's drop the technicalities ...
Aside from the fact that the publication of this insidious nonsense cost the Canadian taxpayers $18,000 for 20,000 copies, it is also an excellent example of a typical episode in this government's well planned con game.
Undoubtedly the next episode will be a further attempt to downgrade the effectiveness of a democratic opposition, and a good hint of what is to come was in the Speech from the Throne when we were told that the government would seek "as a matter of urgency" the "necessary reforms of parliamentary rules".
The key words used foretell what lies ahead. They are the words "matter of urgency" and "necessary", urgent and necessary to tamper further with the rules of this House because of the government's impatience with the democratic process.
How much easier it would be if the cabinet and the Prime Minister were not obliged to come here daily to provide answers to elected representatives of the people. How much easier it would be to run this country whatever way they want if the oral question period was abolished and it was required that all questions be submitted in advance.	,
This government is motivated by a kind of dictatorial complex. Call it of the right or of the left, it makes no difference. It is a government in the hands of a clique whose interests, I believe, ire not synonymous with the best interests of Canada's national unity.
If this was a truly democratic government, surely someone on the front bench opposite would have risen to denounce the words of the Quebec minister of justice spoken earlier this week when he threatened Quebec's English speaking minority by saying that Quebec anglo-

phones are heading for "big disaster" and that he was giving them a "sympathetic warning". He declared:
If the anglophones of Quebec are not ready to accept a minimum measure like Bill 22, they will inevitably provoke a confrontation and reaction that would further the cause of separatism.
There it is, the myth, the lie, the fraud, peddled by this government and its friends. If anyone speaks out in the name of common sense, or stands up for national unity and an end to the fractionalizing of Canada on a racial basis, they are at once a provoker of separatism.
If Canada some day does split apart-and certainly the ignored west, the forgotten Maritimes, and the neglected areas of eastern Ontario, have every justification to think of possible separation-if Canada someday splits into pieces and God hope it never does, this government will go down in history as the author and the instrument of that destruction.
May I say in conclusion, Madam Speaker, that the time is overdue for the great silent bulk of Canadians, nc matter what their mother tongue, to tell this government that we have had enough of its ill conceived, foolish, expensive and disastrous measures of implementing bilingualism; to tell the government that we all want to be just plain Canadians and not hyphenated Canadians, and that we are not prepared to witness the destruction of our country by policies of language and racial confrontation conducted by this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the beginning of my first speech in the House, I would like to paraphrase one of the great men of the antiquity who, returning from a glorious conquest, had exclaimed; "Veni, vidi, vici". It remains indeed that the election of a member at 20 years of age is a victory for the people of a certain age who think that the young people are just good enough to carp about the respective merits of Das Kapital of Karl Marx or the small Red Book of Mao.
With the other members in this House, I would like, on the contrary, to try to give a new impetus to the legislative process and in that context, I wish to thank the electors of Lafontaine for their initiative and their courage, because courage is necessary to turn aside from the beaten track, especially in politics where ultra-conservatism is too often a maxim and the status quo a rule.
I remember a metaphor used by the hon. member for Hamilton-Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) when he was talking about youth in this House. He was comparing youth to a sailboat with the wind of idealism as the motor and reason and common sense as the wheel. In the next few years, I hope to follow a line of conduct inspired from this ideal and it is with this in mind that I rise today to defend some principles which I hold to heart and which come from a certain understanding that I have of our society and the future that I anticipate for it.
Madam Speaker, every day, through the media or in the discussions that we have with other members, we hear about all kinds of problems which are all impossible to solve, including, I must admit, price increases and the various causes of inflation. Much has been said about this, and I am not surprised that the opposition with its legendary opportunism took advantage of this subject during the
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
last electoral campaign. In fact, the problem is much more social than economic or political, and that is what I shall try to prove further on. The fact is that the problem exists and that we have to try and solve it. On this subject, I must immediately give the following explanation; I agree little if at all with the temporary measures suggested by some of our economists who still try to analyze our problems on the basis of assumptions which no longer apply in 1974.
Even though very valid in its details, this budget applies to a temporary period, and I shall not dwell on the external causes of inflation but rather on what we must anticipate in the medium and the long term. To better understand the Canadian economic context, we must realize that Canada is one of the rare countries ready to enter fully a new era, that of a post-industrial society. Solutions developed in the last century no longer apply when it comes to understanding the mechanisms which will control tomorrow's society. The great economic cycles moving on sinusoidal curves are the characteristics of a transitory society undergoing radical changes: such is ours.
We went from the agrarian period to that of industry in the middle of the 19th Century; we are now stepping into that new era I spoke of a while ago, which will be dominated by the third and fourth sectors of our economy.
What then are the main characteristics of that postindustrial society? I quote Jean Fourastie, well known French economist, who wrote in his book "Le Grand Espoir du 20' siecle", and I quote:
By liberating man from tasks inanimate matter can perform for him, the machine must lead him to tasks he alone among created beings can perform: those of intellectual culture and moral perfecting.
We can already see the first effects of that evolution. The third sector, which resists technical progress, will eventually permeate our whole economy and the activities relating to advanced technology limited by its very success, and will absorb only a small part of the labour force. Again, I quote:
The service industries will remain unstable for a long time. Primary and secondary production, the financial value of which will be small though formidable because of its material size, will depend on relatively few workers; a large portion of the population will be made up of indirect workers. One or two hundred workers in a key sector can already threaten the economic system of a nation; in the third sector, a few hundred technicians will be able to deprive millions of human beings of electricity, transportation and food.
This implies the need for a State in a position to make the common good prevail. Inversely, the least hitch in the complex third sector, are oversight or a mistake in the tremendous effort of co-ordination, classification and planning, will result in serious consequences in primary and secondary production.
In fact, such a society is the end result of a process developed in the 19th century during the general industrialization campaign.
This new society overlooks a basic principle, namely "production for production's sake", which can only give rise to never-ending spiral:	price increases, salary
increases, and so on. As a matter of fact, what we must try to do is to make people understand and try ourselves to understand, that at some point, improved living conditions are not evaluated in terms of additional TV sets or tele-

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Lachance
phones for every member of a family, or else in terms of the size and horsepower of a car, but rather in terms of services provided to the people and particularly, the distribution of this affluence, of this opulence of which Galbraith speaks so rightly. Therefore, it is a completely new outlook. Can we draw any conclusions from it?
First of all, as a direct corollary, one must reason with the producers of goods for whom only the sales volume, therefore, the profits, is an indicator of social and economic progress. We must stop trying to adjust supply to demand and fight rather on a new front by adjusting demand to supply. I know that it may look simplistic but it is in fact the mentality of a whole nation that we must try to change.
We must first urge company directors to plan their production instead of giving priority as is the case now to development that I would term as of the "wildcat" sort. We must then change radically the attitude of the consumers themselves. I would like to illustrate briefly a few means of fulfilling those aspirations as related to the rationalizing of industry in Canada, and the setting up of an infrastructure for transportation to regionalize that industrial output. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) understood that priority, and he seems about to introduce a complete restructuration of the means of transportation in Canada.
The immediate effect of that action would be the creation of a planning board with a purely advisory function because I basically believe in the capacity of producers to adapt when it is in their interest. It would be up to that planning board to set up the priorities in the development of areas in line with the long term policies of the government. That already exists at the embryonary stage in the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and I know that the new Federal Business Development Bank will provide advisory services for small and middle businesses.
Still about cost rationalization, a systematic effort should be made to promote the seeding and development of cooperation which has already proven to be an excellent way of serving the often conflicting, but always complementary interests of producers and consumers. Finally, for the consumers themselves, they should be honestly informed so they can learn for themselves the benefits of voluntary restriction.
I would like to say incidentally that it is sheer utopia to hope for a change of attitude in that area as long as the consumer will be the victim of propaganda-and I strongly stress that word-propaganda daily imposed on the consumer through often misleading advertising. I look upon a healthy capitalism where free competition would be effective and whose absolute weapon would be honest information on the true values of the products offered and not a daily and systematic hammering based on mass psychology.
I urge the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) to implement as soon as possible a really efficient code of ethics providing for, among other things, a drastic limitation of budgets allocated to advertising by Canadian companies. That would be a good short-term way to curb inflation, cutting 5 to 10 per cent off the production cost of item offered to consumers.

Finally, any proposal put forward could only be the prelude to the inevitable and long awaited-for final gesture of implementing a guaranteed annual income for all Canadians regardless of age or status. Let us now consider the total cost of government programs of a social nature with identical purposes. Here are some figures: program concerning senior citizens, old age pensions: $2.5 billion; guaranteed income supplement $950 million; pension annuities: $250 million; general social assistance to provinces: over $1 billion; special social assistance: $700 million; family allowances: almost $2 billion; unemployment insurance: $2,250 million. Which gives us an unbelievable total, the grand total of $11,360 million in transfer payments and other revenue support payments.
One can but deplore the administration red tape and daily frustrations citizens are faced with concerning the implementation of these programs, especially when these measures do not meet their hoped-for purpose, which is the case right now. Other mechanisms must be considered.
The guaranteed annual income concept has been gaining momentum these last few years. I quote the following from an article signed by Claude Lemelin which appeared in Le Devoir of November 21:
Within a year, Canada could be provided with a new Federal-provincial guaranteed income program which could replace the numerous income support programs already implemented by Ottawa and the provinces thanks to the progress reported by the Ministers responsible for Social Affairs from the country's 11 governments during the Conference held in the Nation's capital on the 19th and 20th of November.
During this conference three steps were outlined:
1.	A unique and monolithic system, guaranteeing a minimum income to any citizen whose revenues from other sources would not reach a given level, regardless of other socio-economic characteristics;
2.	A two-prong system, which would include first of all a guaranteed income program for workers whose income is inadequate, either because of the size of their families or the seasonal character of their job; and then a full-scale guaranteed income program for those who are either unemployable, unable to find a job or would meet some objective qualification requirements;
3.	A two-prong system identical to the preceding, except that the income guarantee would be provided through tax credits (cashable by non taxpayers) rather than through direct allowances from public funds.
In 1971, the Senate special committee report on poverty already proposed a great number of guaranteed annual income formulas among which I single the following: a negative income tax to be applied nationally on an uniform basis. I quote from the report:
The program would be financed and administered by the federal government which would make uniform cash payments to all economically underprivileged Canadian residents. The payments would depend upon the size and the needs of the family and they would determine a new minimum under which no family would be left alone.
To illustrate this, the poverty line as established in the report is about $7,000 for a family of four. I challenge anyone to claim that the full amount abovementioned is provided through current programmes.
In short and in order to prevent people from regarding me as a so-called "philosopher", I will say I dream of a Canada in which every citizen will have the opportunity of developing his talents and skills, without having to prostitute intellectually, in order to make a living for his family. I dream of a 21st century Canada, which will stop waging constitutional wars and set to work definitely so
November 22, 1974

that everyone may share its good fortune. I dream of a Canada in which we will decide to care for the aged, not by giving them mere pittance and letting under the constant threat of exploitation, but by setting up a rational home care and recreation system. That will be done by programs such as New Horizons and particularly by building homes which are in accordance with the aged and their needs.
Madam Speaker, the days of half-measures are over. The federal government must take the lead and the leadership in all fields with a socio-economic character. Experience has proven that we cannot rely on provincial programs concerning salary supplements. I can assure this House that I am not very proud when a pensioner comes to see me about pension indexation and says to me: "Your programs are all very nice, but why did the provincial government cut my income supplement by an amount equal and sometimes superior to the increase I received from the federal government?" What will be the impact of the new program which is supposed to be in force in 1975? Concerning spouses aged 60 or 65 now on their pension, what will happen when they receive these supplementary amounts? Will the provincial government definitely cut off their income supplement? In that case it is a joke. You cannot fool people that way all the time. We look like fools. No, we must rationalize programs, and the only way I think we can achieve that is by putting all these programs under one level of government, that is the federal government.
Madam Speaker, rebellion is threatening among the poor. It is not sufficient to close our eyes and pray. The time has come to take measures in that area.
In conclusion, let me quote the report of the special Senate committee on poverty, in which is stated the challenge we must face:
Measures must be taken now, if we want to prevent millions of Canadians from continuing to consider life only as a cruel and fierce struggle for survivance. We must set aside our social assistance and service policies and replace them by a program of revenue and financial assistance. We must give the defenseless the hope for a better future.
Madam Speaker, Galbraith wrote about production in his book The Affluent Society:
Furnishing an empty room is one thing. Piling up furniture until the whole place is ready to collapse is another. If the matter of production had been bound to fail, man would have remained doomed to his traditional fate. But if we fail to realize that we have found out the solution and immediately undertake the necessary task, we will be heading for an equally frightful tragedy.
Madam Speaker, I have a dream of happy Canadians. That has been the greatest hope of the 20th century and I have been elected to work at its realization.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that during the two years when I was absent from this House the government, in view of the situation it was facing, would change its thinking. I can see by what has been presented in the budget, and from what has gone on in the House during the present session, that it has not. I had especially hoped that after election night this country would be governed by a new government, and I am disap-
The Budget-Mr. Cadieu
pointed that the wisdom of the voters of the Meadow Lake constituency was not reflected in the election results in the majority of the constituencies in Canada, especially in the constituency of Ottawa-Carleton. If those voters had voted differently, the people of Canada might have been spared the disappointment of this budget.
Be that as it may, I am sure most people in Canada hoped that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) would show leadership and bring forward good ideas. Instead, he has simply added sugar to the same old stew-and with sugar being expensive, he did not add much. If he bought the meat right from the producer, he bought it dirt cheap. One can only say that the Minister of Finance is doing as his fellow ministers are doing, falling flat when faced with his "big moment".
It is difficult to move a truck which is stuck in a rut when a tire is flat. Well, the government is not even trying to move that truck. It thinks that if it leaves the truck there for the winter, the ground will freeze and it can drive the truck away, smiling. Let me tell you that many farmers who own trucks are not smiling, especially if there is livestock in the truck.
It appears that the Minister of Finance has forgotten that it was actually the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who won the election for the government and enabled the minister to keep his job; yet the Minister of Finance, in the budget, hardly mentions anything in which the agricultural industry can show great interest. Certainly that omission does not speak of gratitude.
The Minister of Finance calls for restraint, yet it is evident from the budget figures, to an ordinary farmer or rancher like myself, that the government is suffering from diarrhoea of the purse and intends to cure it with a laxative.
I have seen many of the end results of this ailment, resulting from the way the government has spent so much of the taxpayers' money in a few areas. It is nothing short of deplorable that one quarter of the people in my area do not have television reception; for many the only method of transportation is by air. Unfortunately, most of the residents of my area do not have friends of the sort the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has, Madam Speaker.
I have been told recently that television will not be available to the people of a vast area in the northwestern part of Saskatchewan comprising Canoe Narrows, Beau-val, Pinehouse, lie a la Crosse, Buffalo Narrows, Patuanak, Dillon, Portage la Loche and Tumor Lake, until 1976. In 1972 I was told it would be available in 1974. I wonder what I will be told in 1976.
We should bear in mind that lie a la Crosse is one of the oldest settlements in Saskatchewan. It was this government that destroyed the people's chance to have television reception in this area as long as nine years ago. The radar towers and equipment which were put there at no cost to this government were destroyed. The CBC has showed interest in this equipment. It was an asset with regard to bringing television to this vast area. The radar tower at Fort Black was reduced to scrap for no reason whatsoever.

November 22, 1974
The Budget-Mr. Cadieu
We realize what television would do for the people in this vast area during the long winter, particularly school children and senior citizens. Do I have to tell the people of that area that the government wants to forget them for another two years? This is going to be very bad news for the people in this part of my constituency.
It was this government that discontinued the Roads to Resources program. Large portions of this area, going into the Athabasca region and the great mining country around Uranium City, are as far away from an all-weather road as they were 10 years ago. This government dropped the Roads to Resources program which was set up by the Diefenbaker government. The area around Uranium City has created enough wealth that it should have had an all-weather road leading into it long ago.
I could go on at great length about the shortcomings of the government with regard to the north country. Unless some changes are made, this budget will be pretty slim picking for the people of that area.
There is a terrible problem in western Canada with regard to agriculture. We saw what happened a few years ago to the pork producers in the west. They were put out of business. Today the beef producers are in a deplorable situation. A lot of this has been caused by government meddling.
Only a few months ago the government was advocating that farmers diversify and go into beef cattle. I do not know where the government researchers were, but I know the predicament in which the western farmers find themselves today. We know what the beef producers are doing in eastern Canada. We saw an example of that not too long ago.
There have been many farm starts in my constituency. People were encouraged to go into beef cattle. In order to do this they borrowed money at a high rate of interest. Many who bought breeding stock last spring cannot get back one quarter of what they paid.
Are we to look forward to the same kind of situation for our grain producers? Just recently the minister in charge of the wheat board introduced a two-price system for wheat. Our party has advocated that for many years. We worked hard for a two-price system. However, today the government wants a two-price system with a maximum price for wheat consumed locally. It did not call in the producers or the farm organizations to discuss setting a price for a period of seven years. At the rate inflation is going in this country, I wonder whether $3.25 a bushel will be adequate in seven years. Who knows? Why would the government force through such a bill without first consulting those who are very much concerned? It is very injust. I think the opposition has forced the government to take another look at this. I think it will now call in the producers and farm organizations to discuss this bill. There are many such situations in western Canada. The people there will certainly not be happy with this budget.
We hear a lot today about rail line abandonment. In my area many lines have never been completed. If some of these lines had been completed, they would be on a paying basis. How can a rail line that has not been completed, pay? There is still a gap in the line, and now the government is talking about abandonment. This makes me think

of our forefathers who pioneered this country. They advocated the. .ail lines. However, even at this late state the lines have not been completed and, as I say, now the government is talking about abandonment.
Everyone in western Canada knows that grain can be moved much cheaper by rail than by truck. Therefore I do not know why the government is determined to go hog-wild into rail line abandonment. The people concerned should have some say about this.
There are many other items I could deal with, especially northern development. The government should take a close look at the Roads to Resources program. It should also provide television for these people I have mentioned. They are entitled to it. These people have spent the greatest part of their lives in that area. Surely they should have the right to television.
I took notice of what the minister had to say in his budget about housing. For years we have been asking for the removal of the sales tax on building materials and at a time when so many young people are in need of homes I do not understand why it should be retained, even in part. It is true the Minister of Finance has agreed to reduce it, but when one considers the expense of maintaining the bureaucracy needed to collect the tax at 5 per cent, it might have been far better to have abolished it altogether.
The whole budget is ill-conceived as far as I am concerned, speaking for the constituency of Meadow Lake.

The tax reduction on building materials is an excellent measure, I believe, but that tax should have been removed completely. A mere 6 per cent reduction in the tax on building materials will not be enough to incite those who wish to build a home to avail themselves of this reduction, because financial institutions are less and less eager to lend money to young people. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to thank all hon. members for their courtesy in enabling us to adjust our procedures to the statement to be made.
In February, 1973, I announced that the National Energy Board would hold a public hearing "in order to provide opportunity for interested parties to be heard as to the appropriate methods for protecting the public interest in respect of oil exports over the longer term". After preparatory work, notice of the board's hearings with respect to this matter was given on July 5, 1973 and companies and interested groups were asked to file briefs with the board by October 15. Subsequently, the board held hearings in Calgary, Vancouver and Ottawa, terminating on May 2, 1974. '
The board, after carefully considering all submissions, testimony and argument presented, set out its findings in a report to me on the matter of the exportation of oil which it submitted under section 22 of the National Energy Board Act. Under section 23 of the act, reports of the board made under Part II may be made public with the approval of the minister and, having regard to the importance of this report, I decided that it should be made public so that all Canadians may be aware of the oil supply and demand outlook in Canada, and of the need to take further action with respect to oil exports.
The government accepts the board's finding that steps should be taken to reduce exports of oil with a view to providing additional protection for Canadian requirements. To this end the board intends to modify immediately its licensing procedure.
The government accepts the board's recommendation for a new export control system. However, in view of the impending requirements for the Montreal market, I intend to seek early consultation with the producing provinces with a view to reducing exports more sharply than under the board's recommended formula. The board allocated
250,000	barrels per day for the Montreal market from 1975 onward but proposed that these supplies be declared surplus to Canadian requirements-and therefore eligible for export-until the Montreal line comes onstream in 1976. I intend to discuss with the provinces the advisability of "shutting in" these supplies beginning in mid-1975, rather than considering them surplus to Canadian requirements for export purposes until the line is completed in 1976.

November 22, 1974
Energy
This would result in a reduction of exports to a level of about 650,000 barrels per day for the latter part of 1975, compared to an export level of some 800,000 barrels per day that would otherwise be in effect.

Evidence produced before the National Energy Board during its hearing and its appraisal of this evidence indicated an inevitable decline in producibility of indigenous crude oil commencing next year and continuing in the 1980's, when frontier oil and larger quantities of oil sands output are expected to become available.
Based on present supply and demand trends, there is a forecast deficiency in supply to the domestic market served by Canadian oil in early 1982 which would grow to
200,000	barrels a day by late 1983. In the face of this prospect the Board decided to adopt a new procedure to determine the level of oil exports, based on a formula by which the volume of crude oil available for export licensing during a given year will be related to oil producibility, demand for Canadian use, and a conservation expectation as estimated for that year. The volume of oil exports thus computed would be reduced by a factor which would become more severe as the estimated period of self sufficiency decreased.

The government decided against an immediate and complete discontinuance of oil exports because cessation of exports would provide for sufficient producibility for only a few months additional to that provided by the phased reduction of exports approved by the cabinet. That is, an immediate halt to exports would extend sufficient deliver-ability for about two and a half years while the government's decision to phase down exports in line with the board's recommendations will extend the period for about one and a half years. As I stated, it is my intention to seek consultations with the producing provinces with an aim to extending this period to two years by beginning the phase down of exports next year and in 1976.
An immediate halt to exports would be disruptive to Canadian-United States trade relations. It would deprive certain northern U.S. refineries and their communities of the Canadian crude oil on which they have traditionally relied.
In Canada a sudden and complete reduction of current exports would deprive industry of a major source of cash flow required to find the higher cost reserves of the frontier areas. It would also idle a portion of the capacity of producing facilities which have been financed over the past few years. There would be a major impact on the income of the oil producing provinces, on the oil service industries, and a major effect on Canada's foreign exchange.
In adopting its new procedure the board will identify the volume of allowable oil exports for a period of at least one year, but annual average levels .will be adjusted to account for immediate supply and demand factors by issuing monthly export licences, as at present. Hearings will be held periodically to receive evidence with respect to the potential producibility of Canadian oil, the domestic demand for indigenous feed stocks, and the effects of conservation on Canadian consumption and surplus.

While the board is forecasting that by 1982 there will not be enough crude oil production in Canada to meet the Canadian market demands which are now served by Canadian oil production, plus 250,000 barrels a day for Montreal, this outlook can be altered not only by the board's proposed export control formula but also by greater attention by all levels of government, and by all citizens, to conservation measures in the use of energy. The federal government will announce this winter a series of programs designed to conserve all forms of energy.
In 1960, when the federal government launched the national oil policy, the export level was about 100,000 barrels a day. By 1970 exports had risen to 670,000 barrels a day. The rapidly growing deficiency in the United States in the early years of this decade created a sharply increased demand for Canadian crude, and exports rose to the 1.1 million barrel a day level by 1973 when the government instituted export controls. This control system has enabled the government to reduce exports, which for 1974 have averaged 900,000 barrels per day.
By the 1980's we can expect a resurgence in production as the frontier areas and the oil sands are opened up. At the same time our capability in nuclear energy production will also become very significant. Thus the energy supply outlook for the long term is promising. The challenge before us is to maintain a high degree of self-sufficiency in the intervening years, and this new regime of oil export control I have announced today is designed to attain that objective.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to table copies, in the two official language, of the report of the National Energy Board, "In the Matter of the Exportation of Oil".

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the report by the National Energy Board entitled "The Matter of the Exportation of Oil" demonstrates to this institution that the National Energy Board can produce a very useful document whenever it is requested to do so. I welcome the National Energy Board back to its function as laid down in the act of 1959, namely, of advising the government and the people of Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext:
I have read the report and I cannot help but compare it with the report we received from the government last July entitled, "A National Oil Policy for Canada". When I look at the charts in that volume on supply and the optimism and the expectations they represent, I get the impression that the figures we read in this report today are going to be much more useful to the government in planning future policy.
I cannot understand for the life of me, in view of what is in this report on the exportation of oil, presented to the House today, why the government kept it secret so long. It would have been just as useful two weeks ago, and we might have avoided a lot of the misery the members of this House had to endure this last two or three weeks. I think it will become clear in my remarks why that is so, Mr. Speaker.
I am not going to quote extensively from the report, but would like to refer to two short passages, the first one
November 22, 1974

dealing with supply in barrels per day. I want the House to listen to the conclusion reached by the National Energy Board after it heard all the submissions of industry and its own experts. It reads:
Various studies of geologically potential oil, gas and other resources leave little doubt that there are abundant deposits in widely scattered areas of Canada. The conversion of known resources, such as the oil sands and heavy oils, and inferred or potential resources, such as are expected in the frontier areas, into established reserves will require technological progress but, more importantly, will require favourable economic conditions for development, production and transportation. There is also a major problem in respect of timing. However, given sufficient lead-time and proper economic incentives, there is a good prospect that Canada could become self-sufficient in energy for a long period.
In view of that conclusion there is no need to terrorize the people of Canada into thinking that our future is opaque and dismal.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext: Would the hon. member please give me the page number from which he quoted?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext:
Page 2-14.
Then again in chapter 5, page 15, speaking this time on the subject of exports, the report reads:
Given the size, nature and timing of a possible supply-demand intersection, as set out in section 4 of this report, the board is of a view that policies of all levels of government, of the financial community, and of the industry itself must be such as to ensure that adequate rates of return and cash flows are available.
That is the view of the board that we in parliament set up to advise us on the public interest in matters of energy. I repeat again, as the minister has stated in his own statement and as the report states, that Canada needs a continuation of imports into this country to keep our own economy healthy and to keep our energy situation healthy, particularly in the next 10 years. Also, if we are to achieve this type of situation where our industry is healthy, we will have to provide favourable economic conditions. The question is, how? I will come back to this in a moment.
But before I go into that I would like to talk about imports. On October 3 in the House I made a proposal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) which he has promised to consider, that Canada should offer its hospitality to all countries of the world, both importers and exporters of oil, presumably some time next year, with the purpose of bringing a rule of law into world prices of oil, and also to give us the framework within which the countries of the world allocate supplies instead of this being done by international oil companies.
As I stated, the Prime Minister promised to consider that proposal. The reason I hesitated in asking if he has made a decision is that I requested the Arab nations in OPEC to make their representations to the Secretary ,of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) in Canada indicating to him, and hopefully through him to the Prime Minister, that the Arab nations consider this proposal in a favourable light. I have great hopes that even though we do not have ambassadorial strength in all the Arab countries, and even though our own nation does not go to see
Energy
the Arabs, that the Arab nations will come and see us, expressing a will to join in such an international undertaking.
An international commodity agreement should have been in place these last 50 years. Instead, we have had to rely on the good graces and efficiency of the international oil cartel to set our prices and allocate our supplies.
Secondly, in regard to favourable economic conditions, I do not think there is a person on either side of this House who, in his heart, does not know that there should be an end to this war on the provinces. We have to realize that provincial governments are the voice of the people of an area. You cannot go over them with unilateral actions, repudiating agreements not only with provincial premiers and provincial ministers, but with industry.
I suggest that if we are going to follow the recommendations in the exportation of oil document provided by the National Energy Board we should return to the traditional Canadian way of working out our federal system, namely, consulting with our provinces in the running of this country.
By consultation, Madam Speaker, I do not mean just the phasing down procedures which the minister has stated he is going to start in consultation with the producing provinces. I am not talking about that itty bitty little bit of technical detail. I am talking about the whole energy picture, and that includes price and the staging of price increases; it includes a cushion for the consumers. If there is injustice, or if extra sacrifice is demanded from the producer provinces greater than the ordinary Canadian should have to bear to maintain these national purposes, the principle of quid pro quo should still apply as it applied at the time of the drafting of the British North America Act without which there would be no agreement, and as it did in the Alberta and Saskatchewan Natural Resources Act of 1930. Without that agreement we would not have made the progress we did make in this country in the last 107 years.
In this whole energy picture we should consider the provinces on the question of exports, the question of imports and, above all, in the matter of taxation, which is the present quarrel. Pipelines should be brought to their attention. It is in our prerogative entirely, but they are providing the energy and we should consult with them.
Above all, in the final industrial strategy people who live in Ontario, in the industrial complex between Sarnia and the eastern townships of Quebec, know that other regions of this country want a chance to share in its wealth, not as a handout through a DREE grant but with their resources giving them comparative advantage. I would suggest that if you consult on this over-all energy picture it would be a tremendous day in the history of Canada.
In view of the minister's attitudes and his actions in the last two or three years, this means he will have to follow the precedent of an illustrious predecessor who was a leader of the Liberal Party. When William Lyon Mackenzie King sat on this side of the House he said he was prepared to "walk in the valley of humiliation". He survived.

November 22, 1974
Energy
I notice today, Madam Speaker, that in. response to a question by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yew-chuk) the Prime Minister said that he was willing to reconsider the petroleum administration bill and the resource sections of the budget that have divided this House. I ask the Prime Minister, through the Minister of Energy (Mr. Macdonald) to give that matter his deepest consideration because, if we do not become flexible again, if we do not treat our provinces as provinces of Canada deserving of consideration, the end will be something most of us do not want to contemplate. I am putting it this way, in terms which can be understood. If we do not agree to create a favourable economic climate, it will be the consumer who will pay the price for our neglect.
Having said that, may I now comment on the proposed oil pipeline. I used to refer to it as the pipeline to Montreal, but now I prefer to speak of it as the pipeline from Montreal to Sarnia. This must be a two-way pipeline. It must be capable of moving oil in both directions if we are to do what the report recommends. We must utilize to the maximum any oil which we acquire on world markets. If the government cannot find a private corporation which is willing to build a pipeline because of uncertainties over guarantees, I think the government, in the interests of this country, must build it itself, even if the pipeline stays empty. It will be there to protect us. It will protect those in the centre of Canada. It will move oil to Sarnia, if necessary, or to Montreal and the eastern areas of the country.
Next I shall speak on the question of export. I think the recommendations of the report are sensible. They come down against cutting off exports completely and recommend, from the beginning, production of about 650,000 barrels a day, plus 250,000 for the Montreal market, giving an average rate of production of 900,000 barrels per day. That should show western producers that there is a future for them in the Canadian market. If the government goes ahead with its proposals, the market will be stable.
I know oil companies are concerned about price, and we hear talk of much confusion and despair. I know that many boards of directors are considering their programs for next year. If the government would only say, "We will consult with the provinces on taxation, sharing of rents, and so on," I think the industry would feel more confident.
On October 21 last I made a suggestion which, if adopted, will give a way out for the provinces, the industry and the federal government. I know my proposal will work because if it will give the federal government more money, provincial governments more money and the industry more money, it will be acceptable. I ask the government to look at that proposal, because I think that it would restore the confidence of the industry in this country. If that confidence is restored, Canada can look forward to a great future; but that future can only be realized if there is cooperation between senior governments.
I will not say much about conservation and the environment, as the report deals with these questions adequately. Incidentally, if the minister intends to turn lights off, I wish he would turn off the lights in the Pearson building.

They are on every night. We can live with the recommendations of the National Energy Board on that subject.
The report does not deal with alternative sources of energy. True, it mentions nuclear sources but does not mention renewable sources of energy. Our neighbour on the North American continent, the United States, is spending $20 billion in a 10-year program developing alternative sources of energy. It is spending at the rate of $2 billion per year. Of that $2 billion it is spending $60 million a year on a biomass program-the minister will tell the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) what that means. According to the information I have, Canada at present is spending about $200,000 a year in this field.
I feel I have dealt adequately with the report, Madam Speaker, to show that it is sufficient grounds for confidence. The report shows that we are justified in our confidence in the future of Canada, even though there is a difficult 10-year period ahead. Canada has before it great opportunities, and the report will do much to enable us to restore our confidence in ourselves. Certainly we must bring frontier oils and tar sand oils on stream between 1985 and 1990; it is a just a question of being sensible in the meantime. I hope the government will take advantage of this report, withdraw the petroleum administration bill and cancel those sections of the budget which would start a war between the federal government and the provinces.
If it does that it will be amazed at how the stock market will react on Monday and succeeding days, and we shall all be pleased at what we in this country can do, once we create a favourable economic climate. We need not despair, Madam Speaker.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT

Madam Speaker, I feel something like a passenger on the Titanic watching the captain re-arranging the seating after having struck the iceberg.
I have only had an opportunity to make a very hasty and cursory examination of this report. I think it is probably more realistic than some of the reports we have had from the National Energy Board. It is certainly much more realistic than some of the estimates that have been made by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources with respect to the life index of oil supplies in Canada. However, I would point out that they are still fairly optimistic and are still making assumptions which, in my opinion, are very dubious.
If I can summarize it quickly, they are suggesting that if we leave our exports to the United States at their present level and continue our present consumption and present imports, the life index of our conventional western oil is 7.3 years. If we cut off our exports as of January 1, 1975, our supplies will last 9.9 years before we will be in a position of non self-sufficiency. If we phase out the exports on a schedule which they have set, we will extend the life of the oil reserves of Canada to some 9.0 years.
I cannot for a moment understand why we should talk about phasing out exports to 1982. The minister said in his statement that he wants to reduce these exports more rapidly than the National Energy Board has suggested. However, as I take it from his statement, all he is proposing to do is have consultations with the provinces with a view to beginning, in the middle of July, to take the

250,000	barrels a day which would be going through the pipeline if the pipeline were there, and retaining that oil rather than making it available for export. That means we save 150,000 barrels a day until such time as the pipeline from Sarnia to Montreal is built. The minister hopefully suggested that that might be in 1976. That is not stepping up the reduction of exports very materially.
It should not be necessary to take seven years to phase out our exports to the United States. I agree with the minister that we cannot cut off those exports all at once. That would be unfair. I think it would call for the measures of retaliation. I have advocated for the past four or five years, and I have said it many times in this House, that we ought to give the Americans notice that we are going to phase them out over a period of three or four years. That would give them time to make arrangements for other sources of supply. I think that should be done. However, I see no reason why this phasing out process should be extended over a seven-year period.
The minister argues this will cause some dislocation in the United States. I want to point out to the minister that it will cause some dislocation in Canada if in 1982 we are not able to meet our own oil needs. Also, I think that three or four years would give the Americans ample time to prepare themselves for any dislocation.
Canadians tend to forget that the Americans have larger supplies of oil than we have and that the Americans import a smaller percentage of their oil requirements than we do.
In the 12 month period ending June 30 last, we exported 60 per cent of our oil production. That is ridiculous in a country which has only a few years of conventional oil supplies left.
I can see no reason why the period for phasing out exports cannot be reduced to three years or, at the most, to four years. The minister raises a question of great importance when he says this will cause hardship to the oil-producing provinces and to the oil industry. That is true, if we phase out exports and lack facilities for sending that oil to eastern Canada. The oil would have to be kept in the ground. But I would think the minister could work out a suitable policy.
I see no reason why payment cannot be made for oil in the ground. I remember that when we did not want to export some of the surplus supplies of natural gas from Saskatchewan, because we knew we would require them, we actually paid those same companies to keep the gas in the ground until we required it. And now, of course, we do require it and are very glad to have it available. I believe the provinces and the industry could be compensated until such time as we can take the oil out of the ground.
We are running close to the line. We shall face a critical situation in 1982. I think the margin allowed by the National Energy Board is too narrow. They are counting heavily on the tar sands coming into production from 1980 on, and they are estimating that the Canadian Oil Sands Company will be producing-it is, indeed, producing now-and that Syncrude will be operating at full capacity, which is dubious, and that Shell will be in production by that time. Shell has not even started. It is supposed to

start next year, or the year after, but there is no guarantee that it will. The whole report is based on the optimistic assumption that from 1980 on we shall be able to count on fairly large supplies of oil from the tar sands.
There is also the assumption that we shall be able to count on oil from the Arctic and from the east coast. But if one examines the report closely, and looks at the figures given by the different companies, one reaches the conclusion that supplies of oil from those two sources can hardly be expected before 1985-1990.
I am disappointed the minister has not told us what policies the government intends to follow to ensure these further supplies of oil when our present conventional supplies are exhausted or near exhaustion. He has delayed making a statement on this report; his statement was held over until the stock market was closed. I do not know why. All the minister is telling us is that the National Energy Board is proposing to phase out our exports over seven years, and that he intends to carry out a public relations campaign to persuade Canadians to preserve petroleum. There is certainly nothing startling about that. What we need to know are the government's policies with respect to ensuring an increase in supplies to meet the critical situation that the National Energy Board has anticipated around 1982.
The National Energy Board assumes, for instance, that in the tar sands one plant will be built every 18 months. That is at least $1 billion per plant, and with inflation we can probably add 50 per cent to that. Not only is it a financial problem, but we have yet to solve the environmental problem. A million barrels a day from the oil sands means that after the oil has been extracted you have to dispose of two million tons of loose oil sand. The environmental problems are tremendous and they have to be faced up to, now and in the future.
Arctic and frontier development will require large sums of money and manpower. What policies has the government to ensure that in only seven years we are going to have from the tar sands, and/or from the Arctic and east coast, adequate supplies of oil to meet the very critical situation that is almost upon us? I think that unless we can get some statements of policy it is very difficult for me to share the optimism either which the minister displays or which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) indicated.
To sum up, Madam Speaker, I think this country is heading into a very critical energy crisis. I think we are in a race against time. I do not like to sound like Cassandra; the only feeling of justification for so doing comes from the fact that Cassandra was right.
As I say, we are heading into a very critical situation and we have only a few years in which, firstly, to conserve the oil we have by reducing our exports, and secondly, to enter into a crash program to develop the tar sands and, if possible, to get oil from the Arctic and the east coast. Keeping in mind that so far we have not discovered any oil of commercial quantity either in the Arctic or off the east coast, we may be leaning on a broken reed. Therefore, our best hope at the moment is to get oil from the tar sands. I have seen no indication of any program that will supply the large sums of money required for that purpose.

November 22, 1974
Energy
This is a race against time, and time in this instance is not on our side.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CURTAIL OIL EXPORTS-TABLING OF NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the National Energy Board report just tabled by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) indicates to the people of Canada that we are on the verge of an energy crisis, an oil crisis more serious in nature than we were told in October of last year. The minister however concluded on an optimistic note.
I find that hard to follow. I remember at the beginning of the session in the fall of 1973, I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources what were our reserves for eastern Canada, and whether there was danger of scarcity during the winter of 1973-74. At that time, the minister answered reserves were adequate and there was no danger whatsoever. Yet a few days later the minister said in a special debate that we were on the verge of a full energy crisis. This optimistic note by the minister now leaves me in doubt. And when I see that known Canadian reserves are adequate for 7.3 years only, even in the assumption of immediate curtailment of exports, this would give only a 2.6-year extension. There comes the immediate conclusion that we must take steps to find other sources of energy.
It is now mentioned in the province of Quebec that the investment in the hydroelectric project now under construction in my constituency will reach the $20 billion level. There is mention of investing some $80 billion in the exploitation of Albertan tar sands and Athabaska heavy oils. In other words, it will take hard cash to get heat. Madam Speaker, I suggest Canadians living now, as those
living in 1980 or 1990, will not be able to repay even the interests on the investments involved in the development of resources needed for industry and everyday life. This makes evident the difficulties we are facing in such undertakings. The multinational oil companies now use the slogan to which we were accustomed by finance companies: "Travel now, pay later".
Some oil companies have followed this pattern. Since last fall, they have been telling us: Pay now for the development which will have to come later. That is what we have been forced into. Prices of gas and home heating oil have increased. Now we have to face these difficulties. Even by taking immediate action in order to reduce exports to the United-States or, at least to phase them down, we will only solve part of the problem which finally will have to be faced: storing 250,000 barrels a day in the area of Montreal until the day when we can use the pipeline which is expected to be built by the fall of 1976. The laying of the pipeline has not started yet, and given the building problems of an undertaking of this kind I, very much doubt that it might be ready then.
Madam Speaker, one thing is sure: We now know what to expect and I believe that the government, with the agreement of the provincial governments, must take immediate action to promote further exploration, not only of oil, but of any form of energy which might be used by Canadians.
